The Trouble with Sandpoint

The through-line of the campaign

Sandpoint is a small frontier town with a great deal of wilderness pressed against it. The trouble began with livestock disappearing from outlying farms. Then came raids on barns and storehouses. Then children began to vanish.

The goblins responsible appear to be coming from the wooded hills beyond the hinterlands, but nobody in Sandpoint knows how many there are, where their chief makes his lair, or why the raids have suddenly become so aggressive.

Mayor Kendra Devron has little money, fewer soldiers, and no one else willing to go looking. The campaign begins with a simple job: clear a goblin warren in the hills and bring home anyone still alive inside.

It will not remain simple for long.

What Is Really Happening

The raids are not random. The goblin chief is dying from a mysterious disease, and his tribe is becoming desperate.

  • The tribe's shaman believes a unicorn's horn can cure the chief.
  • The goblins have already found a unicorn — Silverlance — and struck him with a cursed magical arrow.
  • Silverlance escaped before they could take his horn and is now dying slowly somewhere northeast of the forest.
  • A large goblin hunting party is searching the caves for his lair.
  • The chief's illness is real. The black gem controlling him is a separate problem: it enslaves him, but did not cause the disease.
  • The goblins do not know exactly where he is. Neither do the adventurers.

GM Truth: The Dragon Behind the War

The hidden power behind the campaign is a young black dragon. It has claimed the buried complex and the surrounding frontier as the beginning of its territory, but it is not yet strong enough to rule the region openly without attracting adventurers, soldiers, rival monsters or an older dragon.

So it rules by proxy. The black gem in the Goblin King's eye turns the chief into a puppet. The tribe raids Sandpoint's hinterlands for food, loot and tribute, guards the approaches to the dragon's small hoard, and takes the risks the dragon prefers not to take itself. The unusual twenty-gold payment to the cave sentries comes from that hoard: cheap wages for disposable guards who never need to know what they are really protecting.

Silverlance is the dragon's other problem. A unicorn living in the woods is everything the dragon does not want near its first claimed territory: a source of protection for weaker creatures, a force of purity against corruption, and the sort of wonder that eventually draws heroes. The dragon wanted him gone without revealing itself.

The Goblin King's illness is real, and Silverlance's alicorn genuinely can cure it. The dragon learned this and quietly planted the solution in the Stiltwalker's mind. To the goblins it looked like desperate salvation: find the unicorn, take the horn, save the chief. To the dragon it was a way to turn the tribe's panic into a weapon against Silverlance. It also supplied the cursed arrow—something the goblins could never have made themselves—so the unicorn would die slowly even if he escaped the first hunt.

This explains the dragon's behavior in the finale. It watches from above, avoids a fair fight, uses a puppet rather than ruling openly, and when the puppet is broken it destroys the lair rather than risk itself defending a lost position. "You broke my toy" is not bravado. It is petty ownership. The dragon leaves alive, furious, and convinced the adventurers now owe it a debt.

None of this needs to be spoken aloud. The evidence is enough. The referee simply knows the answer if someone eventually asks why the dragon cared about a unicorn hunt: it wanted the beautiful thing gone, the region farmed, and its claim left undisturbed.

The adventurers begin knowing none of this. Let them discover as much or as little of it as play allows.

The Town of Sandpoint

The campaign hub

Sandpoint is small, poor, and close enough to the wilderness that danger reaches the farms before news reaches the town hall. It has a town hall, a market, one smith, a shrine, a tavern, and a ring of hinterland farms that feed the settlement.

Half a day's walk reaches goblin country. Two days' travel reaches a town large enough to have a proper armoury. Sandpoint's limited supplies are part of the campaign pressure: treasure matters because it buys time, equipment, and people.

Places

  • The town hall. Mayor Kendra Devron's office, a hinterland map marked with raids and missing livestock, and the front steps where important news is announced.
  • The market. Gems, curiosities, and salvage can be sold here at a fair price or nearly. Weapons and armour are thin on the ground.
  • The smith. One forge, competent and slow. Broken weapons can be repaired; ordinary replacements take days.
  • The shrine. A small house of faith where adventurers may seek ordinary religious services, leave offerings, or arrange memorials.
  • The tavern. Porters, torchbearers, hunters, men-at-arms, and would-be adventurers gather here when they are looking for work.
  • The hinterlands. Farms and scattered homesteads surrounding Sandpoint. Rumors, survivors, and new trouble often arrive here first.

Between Expeditions

  • Sell. Gems, salvage, and curiosities turn dungeon loot into usable wealth.
  • Rearm. The smith can repair or replace common gear, but not instantly.
  • Hire. Help can be recruited from the tavern. Reputation affects willingness and price.
  • Report. Mayor Devron pays what Sandpoint can afford and reacts to what the adventurers bring home.
  • Mourn. The shrine will hold a memorial with or without a recovered body.

Sandpoint should remember what the adventurers do. Saved families return to their fields. Repeated raids empty them. Hirelings who come home tell stories. Hirelings who do not come home make the tavern quieter the next time the party starts recruiting.

Running the Campaign

Situations, not a script

The Black Eye of the Goblin King is written for Dragonslayer and assumes descending armor class, roll-under ability checks on a d20, category saves, percentile thief skills, side initiative re-rolled each round, reaction rolls, morale, and dangerous low-level combat.

The adventure does not require a specific party composition. A thief may make some obstacles easier. A cleric or other good-aligned character may have advantages in dealing with Silverlance. An intelligent reader may uncover information others miss. None of those roles should be required to continue the campaign.

Most importantly, later chapters do not dictate earlier outcomes. Silverlance can live or die. Prisoners can escape. Enemies can surrender. Hirelings can survive. Player characters can die. The goblins can win races the party loses. Carry those consequences forward instead of forcing the adventure back onto a recorded path.

Information Discipline

Keep the goblin chief's illness, the shaman's plan, the cursed arrow, and Silverlance's location behind the screen until the adventurers discover them. The tension works because the party begins by thinking it has a simple goblin problem.

Failure Does Not End the Campaign

When the party retreats or loses an objective, change the world. Raids worsen. A wounded enemy moves. A captured goblin escapes with news. A clue goes cold. The next chapter should begin from the new situation rather than pretending the setback never happened.

Campaign Rules

Nine rulings worth knowing before play

Use Dragonslayer normally except where the module says otherwise. These are the few campaign rulings that come up often enough to keep in your head. Less common rulings are collected under Additional Campaign Rulings.

  • Initiative every round. Roll side order at the top of each round. Re-roll ties.
  • Declare spells before initiative. A caster announces the spell and target before the round order is known.
  • Zero is not dead. At exactly 0 hit points, a character is unconscious for 1d6 rounds, then revives at 1 hit point. Below −10 is dead. A dying character saves versus death; a natural 20 is a miracle and returns them to 1 hit point.
  • Morale matters. Check morale when more than half a monster group is down, when its leader falls, or when the fiction gives the survivors a strong reason to run. Roll it in the open.
  • Binding wounds. Ten minutes of rest after a fight restores 1d3 hit points. A night's sleep restores time and spells, but no hit points by itself.
  • Time creates danger. Make an encounter check for each travel leg or roughly every ten minutes spent searching, resting, forcing doors, working locks, or otherwise lingering in a dangerous place.
  • Natural 1s create openings. A character who rolls a natural 1 drops or compromises the weapon as appropriate; bows may snap a string. When a monster rolls a natural 1 in melee, its target gains an immediate free attack.
  • Advantage and disadvantage are ±4. Do not roll a second die. Smaller situational edges may be worth +1 or +2 when the fiction clearly supports them.
  • Let dangerous ideas work. Improvised stunts should carry a visible cost or risk—position, damage, an ability check, a saving throw—then produce a real effect when they succeed.
Prologue · Module SP–1

The Hillside Warren

Six areas · 4–6 adventurers · a rescue, two hazards, and something that should not be here

The Charge

The campaign begins here

Goblins have been taking livestock from the hinterlands. Then children began disappearing.

Mayor Kendra Devron offers 100 gold pieces to any company willing to clear a tunnel complex in the hills half a day's walk from Sandpoint and bring home anyone still alive inside. She has only a crude map showing the hillside and the tunnel mouth. She does not know how many goblins are there or how deep the tunnels run.

The job appears straightforward: go in, kill or drive out the goblins, search for captives, and return to Sandpoint.

It is the first wrong assumption of the campaign.

GM Snapshot

Known to the adventurers: goblins are using a hillside tunnel complex and at least one child may still be alive.

Actually inside: two goblins, a captive farm boy, a flame trap, harmless yellow fungus, dangerous yellow mold, and an intelligent undead creature calling itself the Skeleton King.

The unanswered question: the Skeleton King does not belong to the goblin tribe. Nothing in this dungeon explains who crowned him, why his armor appears from nowhere, or why he chose this place.

Running the Warren

  • Light matters. The dungeon quickly leaves daylight behind. Establish who carries the light source before Area 2.
  • Time matters. Use the campaign's normal dungeon encounter checks for delay, searching, lock work, and extended rests.
  • Do not force the rescue. The farm boy wants out, but how he gets out is the party's decision.
  • Do not explain the Skeleton King. His presence is a campaign thread, not a puzzle with an answer in this room.

Foundry scene · scene-hillside-warren-drawn.json

1

The Tunnel Mouth

Hours of walking bring you to a bald, desolate hillside where little grows. Set into it, low and lopsided, is the dark mouth of a tunnel.

The passage slopes down into the earth. Behind you, daylight narrows to a grey strip. Ahead, the walls open into a chamber.

From somewhere beyond comes a low, wet growl.

Sight
Dust hangs in the entrance light. Bare rock bears tool scars; this passage was dug rather than naturally formed.
Sound
Footsteps return half a heartbeat late. The growl comes from the chamber ahead.
Smell
Cold earth and old dust, with grease and spoiled cooked meat underneath.
Feel
The floor slopes steadily downward. The air grows warmer as the daylight fades.

Tracks. A character studying the dust can tell that small humanoids have moved through here recently, in both directions.

VTT
Start the scene in daylight and remove ambient light as the party descends. Ask who is carrying the active light source and mark that token.
2

The Guard Chamber

The chamber is small and filthy. A low fire smolders inside a ring of stones. Gnawed bones and torn scraps of cloth have been swept against the walls.

One goblin crouches beside the fire with a roasted sheep's leg in one hand and a notched shortsword close beside the other.

Another lies in a heap of filthy blankets near the wall.

Sight
Two exits lead deeper: west toward a lived-in smell of hay and mold, east behind a curtain of grey cobwebs.
Sound
Fat spits in the fire. The sleeping goblin snores through its nose.
Smell
Woodsmoke, roasting mutton, rancid grease, and unwashed goblin.
Feel
The room is warm after the entrance passage. Grease makes the stone near the fire slick.

Goblin Guards (2)

Small humanoid · AC 6 · hit on 14 before bonuses · 4–7 hp each · attack +1 · shortsword or hand axe 1d6 · XP 7 each

The waking goblin reacts according to surprise and the party's approach. The second begins asleep unless noise has already alerted the room. Once half the group is down, surviving goblins check morale.

If captured or cornered, a goblin can bargain in broken Common. It knows three useful things: a human boy is caged to the west; the eastern hall "burns thieves"; and something it calls "the Bone King" waits below.

Treasure. One goblin carries 7 gp and a glass vial of red liquid with HEAL scratched into the cap. It is a potion of healing restoring 1d8+1 hit points.

Exits. West leads to Area 3. East leads to Area 4 and is clogged with old cobwebs that burn away easily.

VTT
Place both goblins before the scene begins. The sleeping guard should be visibly prone if the party enters quietly; alert it normally if the party makes enough noise.
3

The Cage

A plain wooden door hangs half open. Beyond it, the smell of mold is strong enough to taste.

Most of the room is taken up by an iron cage floored with rotting hay. A bruised, exhausted boy lies curled in the middle of it.

On the far wall, an iron key hangs from a hook — beyond the reach of anyone inside the cage.

Sight
Several bars are bent outward, as though something larger than the boy was once kept here. Scratch marks score the lower half of the door.
Sound
Water drips behind the wall. The boy's breathing is shallow and fast.
Smell
Wet hay, mold, urine, and old food.
Feel
The iron key is cold and damp. The hay squelches under pressure.

The farm boy was taken from the fields several days ago. He believes the goblins intended to eat him and desperately wants to return home. He has heard them mention the Skeleton King and is afraid of whatever lives below.

The key is not trapped.

The hidden mace. Beneath the hay is a serviceable mace the boy managed to keep hidden from the goblins. If freed, he shows the party where it is. A careful search of the cage also finds it.

Getting him home. The boy is frightened and weak, not suicidal. He will leave alone if the party believes the route is safe, wait near the entrance if instructed, or remain with the group if they insist. Do not choose for them.

VTT
The mace is deliberate equipment placement: bludgeoning is especially effective against the Skeleton King. Do not call attention to that connection.
4

The Hall of Yellow Fungus

Beyond the cobwebs lies a broad chamber scattered with gold coins. Pale yellow fungus grows in stalks, knuckles, and sagging shelves across the floor.

Above an open archway on the far side, a stone devil's face has been carved into the wall. Its mouth hangs open.

Beyond the arch, rough stairs descend into darkness.

Sight
The coins are scattered too evenly to look accidental. The devil's carved eyes point toward the floor rather than toward the doorway.
Sound
The fungus gives a dry papery rustle when the air moves. Otherwise the room is unnaturally still.
Smell
Dry and yeasty, almost like bread, over the mineral smell of scorched stone.
Feel
The fungus compresses like wet bread. Stone near the arch is warmer than the rest of the room.

The flame trap. A tripwire runs low through the fungus among the coins. Spotting it requires a Wisdom check. A character who first studies the fan-shaped scorch marks beneath the devil's face gains +4 to the check.

Triggering the wire blasts the coin-strewn half of the room with flame. Everyone in the cone takes 2d6 fire damage, with a save versus breath weapon for half. The mechanism fires once and is then spent.

The fungus is harmless. Cutting, touching, or burning it has no dangerous effect.

Treasure. The scattered coins total 9 gp.

VTT
Put the coins on the map before the party enters and pre-load the flame cone. The soot, warm stone, carved mouth, and unnatural coin placement are the trap's warnings.
5

The Dripping Cavern

The old stairs end in a natural cavern. Stalactites hang from the ceiling and broken stone rises from shallow pools of black water.

A narrow crack splits the far wall, just wide enough for a person to pass sideways.

From somewhere beyond it comes the dry rattle of bone against bone.

Sight
Light doubles in the pools. A pale yellow crust grows across part of the floor, similar in color to the harmless fungus above.
Sound
Water drips from several places. Beneath it, the rattling from beyond the crack comes and goes with deliberate pauses.
Smell
Wet limestone. Near the yellow patch is a faint sour odor like spoiled flour.
Feel
Cold water seeps through boots. Dry, stale air moves out of the crack from the chamber beyond.

Yellow mold. This growth is dangerous. A Wisdom check notices the difference before anyone steps into it. A character who explicitly studies the floor or compares it with the harmless fungus in Area 4 recognizes that something is wrong without a roll.

If disturbed, the mold bursts into a 10-foot cloud of spores. Anyone caught in it must save versus poison or take 2d6 damage and become sickened for one turn. Fire destroys the patch.

Terrain. The pools count as difficult terrain. Stalagmites provide cover.

The crack. The rattling comes from Area 6. A character listening at the opening can tell that something beyond is moving even though it should not be breathing.

VTT
Keep the mold hazard hidden until it is spotted or disturbed. The yellow color is a callback, not the only clue: its crusted texture and sour smell distinguish it from the harmless fungus above.
6

The Throne of Bones

The crack opens into a high chamber. On the far side, stone steps rise to a low platform supporting a throne made from bones — femurs, ribs, and finger joints fitted together and studded with diamonds and rubies.

A skeleton sits upon it.

A longsword rests beside one bony hand. Its blade gives off a faint light of its own.

The skull turns toward you. Red fire blooms in its empty eye sockets.

Sight
As the skeleton rises, golden plates appear around its bones piece by piece. A heavy crown forms last. The throne's gems are physically set into the bone.
Sound
Armor locks into place with hard metallic claps. Its voice is dry and articulate, with no breath behind it.
Smell
Nothing. After the wet, moldy caverns, the chamber is disturbingly sterile.
Feel
The temperature drops as soon as the red light enters its eye sockets.

The Skeleton King speaks. He is arrogant, intelligent, and perfectly willing to answer questions with insults, half-truths, or questions of his own. He refers to the goblins above as servants but does not explain why he is here or who made him king.

If the adventurers have killed the guards, he may greet them with: "So. Sandpoint sends grave-robbers now. You have slain my little servants. Come closer and see what crown they served." Adjust his words to what the party has actually done.

The Skeleton King

Medium undead · target to hit 12 before bonuses · 14 hp · attack +2 · enchanted longsword 1d8+1

Golden plate. His armor manifests as he rises and vanishes when he is destroyed.

Bone body. Bludgeoning attacks gain +4 to hit. Slashing and piercing attacks deal half damage. Describe the difference before stating the rule.

High ground. While fighting from the dais, apply the campaign's normal high-ground advantage.

For a larger or stronger party, give him a second attack rather than additional hit points. Keep the encounter sharp and dangerous rather than turning him into a sack of wounds.

Before initiative. The transformation is visible and takes long enough for the adventurers to react. They may draw weapons, reposition, retreat to the crack, rush the dais, or attempt to speak. Once someone attacks or the moment clearly passes, roll initiative.

Defeat. At 0 hit points, the red light in his eyes goes out, the golden armor and crown vanish, and the remaining bones collapse into dust.

Treasure. His sword remains as a +1 longsword. The throne holds 4 diamonds and 6 rubies worth a total of 250 gp to the right buyer.

No crown. Searching the dust finds no crown and no mechanism that explains the armor.

The campaign thread. Nothing in the Hillside Warren explains a crowned, articulate undead creature occupying a goblin tunnel. Leave that question unanswered.

VTT
The dais is meaningful terrain. Give the Skeleton King room to descend, be surrounded, or force the party into the narrow approach. Do not lock the doors or prevent retreat.

Returning to Sandpoint

The apparent victory

If the adventurers cleared the warren, Mayor Devron pays the promised 100 gp. If they rescued the farm boy, his family receives him in the hinterlands and the party's reputation improves immediately.

The gems can be sold through Sandpoint's market. The glowing sword is plainly magical even if the characters cannot yet identify every property it possesses.

For a few days, the town has reason to believe the problem is solved.

Then the raids begin again.

They are larger, better organized, and aimed directly at the farms that feed Sandpoint. That is the opening situation of Part I: The Hunting Party.

If the Party Retreats

The warren does not reset. Surviving goblins become alert, the farm boy remains in danger, and the Skeleton King continues to wait below. Mayor Devron will still pay for the job if the adventurers return and finish it, but news of the failed attempt spreads through town.

If the Farm Boy Dies

The campaign continues. His family becomes a visible cost of the goblin raids, and Mayor Devron's urgency in Part I becomes harder rather than softer.

If the Skeleton King Is Left Alone

Nothing forces the party to fight him. The goblin warren can be cleared without solving the mystery below. Leave him as an unresolved threat and decide later whether his survival matters when the campaign returns to the question of who — or what — placed him there.

Part One

The Hunting Party

Six scenes · a hard skirmish · a captured messenger · the race begins

The Charge

The quiet after the Warren does not last

For a few days after the Hillside Warren is cleared, Sandpoint begins to believe the trouble may be over.

Then the raids resume.

This time the goblins are not stealing from isolated hillsides. They are striking the hinterland farms that feed the town: livestock butchered in fields, storehouses broken open, fences burned, families abandoning outlying homesteads before they are next.

Mayor Kendra Devron has reached a harder conclusion. Clearing one warren accomplished nothing. The goblin chief has to die.

The problem is that nobody in Sandpoint knows where he is.

GM Snapshot

Known to the adventurers: goblin raids have worsened since the Warren was cleared, and the chief must be somewhere beyond the farms.

Actually happening: the goblin chief is dying. The shaman believes a unicorn's horn can cure him. Silverlance has already been struck by a cursed arrow, and a larger goblin war band is searching the northeastern hills for his lair.

What this chapter must reveal: the chief's illness, the wounded unicorn, and the fact that the goblins are searching for him too. How the adventurers obtain that information is allowed to vary.

The adventure begins as an investigation with almost no lead. It ends as a race.

Scene Key

Five scenes and the moment the campaign changes direction

1

The Mayor's Office

A runner finds you a few days after the Warren and asks you to come to the town hall.

Kendra Devron has a map spread across her desk. New marks have been made across the farms outside Sandpoint — too many of them, and several are fresh.

"The raids never stopped," she says. "They got worse."

She puts one finger down on the ring of farms around the town.

"They've moved into the hinterlands now. These people feed Sandpoint. We cannot keep emptying holes in the ground while whoever commands them sends more."

She looks around the table.

"Find their chief. Kill him. End this."

Sight
A hinterland map crowded with fresh ink marks. Devron has circled the newest raids rather than erasing the old ones.
Sound
A clerk in the next room reading damage claims aloud: livestock, grain, fencing, missing people.
Smell
Ink, floor wax, cold tea, and rain-damp wool from farmers waiting outside.
Feel
The uncomfortable realization that the first victory bought Sandpoint only a few quiet days.

What Devron knows

  • The Warren was not the source of the raids. It was only one goblin position.
  • The newest attacks are concentrated in the hinterlands and along the country beyond them.
  • No one in town knows the chief's location, the size of his tribe, or the route to his lair.
  • There is no reliable goblin guide or captured scout waiting conveniently in a cell.

The first objective is therefore simple: search the raided country, find fresh goblin sign, and follow it until something useful turns up.

Hirelings are optional. Porters, torchbearers, men-at-arms, and other help may be recruited using Sandpoint's normal services. Do not require the party to take anyone, and do not create hirelings merely so a later chapter can kill them.

Questions and preparation. Let the players decide when to leave, what supplies to bring, whether to question farmers, and whether to recruit help. None of those choices are wrong. The search still leads toward the ford, but good preparation should matter when the fighting starts.

VTT
Use the Sandpoint hub rather than a special encounter map. Put the hinterland map on screen and let the players choose their preparations before moving to the regional sketch.
2

The Quiet Hills

Beyond the last farms the country opens into long rolling hills. Grass brushes your boots and the forest ahead is loud with birdsong, insects, and frogs calling from every damp hollow.

The signs of Sandpoint fade quickly. No wagon ruts. No fresh-cut stumps. No chimney smoke. Only the hills, the treeline, and whatever has been moving between them.

Sight
Grass to mid-shin and mostly unbroken. Far behind, the roof of the last farmstead is the final thing made by human hands.
Sound
Birdsong layered over frogs and insects until it becomes a single wall of ordinary wilderness noise.
Smell
Hot grass, crushed mint underfoot, and resin from the pines ahead.
Feel
Sun on the back of the neck and the pleasant early miles of a walk before packs begin to feel heavy.

Establish the sound here. The wildlife is not decoration. The players need to notice how normal and noisy the country is so the silence at the ford means something.

Signs of the raids. If the party actively searches, give them evidence without requiring a roll: a burned shepherd's hut scratched with goblin marks, a butchered sheep with only the choicest meat taken, or a weathered child's shoe well beyond the farms. None reveals the chief's location, but all confirm they are moving through active goblin country.

Marching order. Ask for it before the ford. Include any hirelings, animals, or pack carriers the party chose to bring.

A raided hinterland farm — 26 × 22 · drop in wherever the party goes looking for signs

Foundry scene · scene-raided-farm.json

VTT
This is travel, not an encounter. Keep it brief. Its job is to establish distance, sound, marching order, and the sense that the party is searching rather than following a marked quest trail.
3

The Ford

The land drops toward a shallow stream. Cold water runs over smooth stones and the easiest crossing is obvious.

On the far bank, halfway through the climb out, something changes.

The wildlife has stopped.

No birds. No frogs. No insects close enough to hear. Only the stream behind you.

Ahead, the ground rises into a low embankment with rough natural steps in the stone. Beyond the top lies a clearing at the edge of the forest.

Voices carry from up there — harsh, guttural, and arguing.

Sight
Fresh mud on the far bank has been churned by several small feet moving toward the clearing.
Sound
The missing birds are more noticeable than the goblin voices. The party's own splashing suddenly sounds far too loud.
Smell
Cold water and wet stone. Downwind, something rank and animal.
Feel
A light breeze moves from the stream toward the clearing, carrying scent up the embankment.

The wind matters. Characters who climb directly toward the voices may observe the clearing, but the wolf there can catch their scent before they get long to study it.

Reward an alternate approach. A party that notices the wind and circles downwind may approach more carefully and gains an additional round to observe, position themselves, or attempt an ambush. Do not force the obvious confrontation if the players earn a better one.

Tracks. Anyone examining the mud can tell at least four or five small humanoids and one four-legged animal passed this way recently. The trail leads directly to Scene 4.

The Ford and the Forest-Edge Clearing — 28 × 30 · Scenes 3 and 4 on one map

Foundry scene · scene-ford-and-clearing.json

VTT
State the breeze before asking how the party approaches. Once they crest the rise or otherwise gain sight of the clearing, reveal Scene 4.
4

The Forest-Edge Clearing

Several goblins occupy the clearing ahead. They wear mangy furs and battered shields and carry hand axes better suited to butchering than soldiering. A lean grey wolf prowls among them.

The largest goblin is shouting at a smaller one. The smaller goblin keeps pointing northeast and talking too quickly.

The larger goblin finally steps forward and clubs him across the head with the flat of its axe.

The messenger drops and does not move.

Then the wolf raises its muzzle.

Sight
Grass trampled flat from recent use. The unconscious messenger lies near the center of the clearing. Dense forest closes around the far edge.
Sound
Goblin argument, the crack of the axe haft against bone, then a low wolf growl that may become a howl.
Smell
Wet fur, rancid grease, smoke, and unwashed goblin.
Feel
Loose stone on the embankment. The stream lies downhill behind the party, making a direct retreat awkward but not impossible.

Encounter: Hunting Crew

The clearing contains one goblin boss, two goblin hunters, a wolf, and the unconscious messenger Norc.

Goblin Boss

Small humanoid · target to hit 14 before bonuses · 7–9 hp · attack +2 · hand axe 1d6+1 · morale 9 · XP 14

Discipline by fear. The boss tries to keep the hunters between itself and the most dangerous melee fighter until the line breaks.

Finisher. If an enemy is helpless and within reach, the boss will attempt a coup de grâce rather than politely changing targets.

Goblin Hunters (2)

Small humanoid · AC 6 · target to hit 14 before bonuses · 4–7 hp each · attack +1 · hand axe 1d6 · morale 7 · XP 7 each

They use the embankment, trees, and one another for advantage. They will flank exposed targets and prefer lightly armored enemies when given a choice.

Wolf

Medium beast · target to hit 13 before bonuses · 12 hp · bite 1d6 · morale 6 · XP 36

Scent. Unless the party approached downwind or otherwise concealed its scent, the wolf detects them before a prolonged observation is possible.

Drag down. An attack roll of 18–20 knocks the target prone in addition to dealing damage.

The wolf attacks the nearest immediate threat and changes targets when that threat drops. It does not execute helpless enemies.

Terrain

  • Natural steps: the easiest route up the embankment and a useful choke point.
  • Embankment: creatures fighting from above gain the campaign's normal high-ground benefit.
  • Treeline: provides cover and an escape route for fleeing goblins.
  • Stream: shallow enough to cross but turns a rushed retreat into difficult footing.

Norc is not plot-armored. He begins unconscious and is plainly still breathing to anyone who looks closely. A stray area attack, deliberate execution, or other consequence can kill him.

Do not let his death break the campaign. Norc delivered the shaman's urgent message just before the boss struck him. Any goblin from this crew who survives long enough to be questioned knows the essential news about the chief, the wounded unicorn, and the larger hunt. Norc simply knows it most clearly.

Morale. Check when half the fighting goblins are down or when the boss falls. A survivor may flee into the forest, surrender, or fight on according to the roll.

Treasure. The goblins carry 9 sp between them. Their axes and shields are crude but usable.

VTT
Use a tactical map with the stream along one edge, the embankment across the middle, natural steps through it, the clearing above, and trees on the far side. Place Norc prone before initiative so the players can see that one goblin is already down.
5

Aftermath & the Messenger

The clearing grows quiet again by degrees. The stream keeps moving below the embankment. Birds begin returning to the trees one at a time.

If the unconscious goblin still lives, he eventually stirs, sees the bodies around him, and immediately raises both empty hands.

"Don't kill messenger!" he blurts in rough Common. "Norc is messenger. Norc tells. Norc tells everything."

Sight
Blood darkening the trampled grass, abandoned shields, and a frightened goblin trying very hard to appear harmless.
Sound
Birdsong returning cautiously. Norc talks fast enough to trip over his own Common.
Smell
Iron, crushed grass, wet fur, and the smoke of a small campfire.
Feel
The delayed shaking and exhaustion that arrive after a fight once nobody is actively trying to kill you.

Recovery. If the party uses the campaign's binding-wounds rule, ten minutes here restores 1d3 hit points normally. The interrogation need not wait for this if the players are in a hurry.

What Norc knows

Norc is frightened, concussed, and eager to survive. He does not require torture, elaborate intimidation, or a successful roll to reveal information he believes may keep him alive.

  1. The goblin chief is dying of a disease.
  2. The tribe's shaman believes a unicorn's horn can cure him.
  3. The goblins wounded a unicorn called Silverlance with a special magical arrow yesterday morning. They believe the cursed wound is killing him slowly.
  4. A larger goblin war band is already northeast of here, searching the cave-pocked hills along the forest edge for Silverlance.
  5. The goblins do not know where Silverlance's lair is. They are searching rather than marching to a known destination.

Why Norc was struck. He had just delivered the shaman's order to abandon this patrol and rejoin the larger hunt. The boss answered his frantic insistence with the flat of an axe.

If Norc is dead or escaped

Any surviving member of the hunting crew knows the first four facts because Norc delivered the message before the fight. A captured goblin is less articulate and does not know Silverlance's name, but can still point northeast and explain that the shaman wants the wounded white horned beast before it dies.

If no goblin survives to be questioned, the party can still follow the crew's fresh trail northeast. This route leads into Part II, but the players begin the race without understanding exactly what they are chasing. The first contact with the larger war band or clear unicorn sign should reveal the missing facts rather than stopping the campaign.

What happens to Norc

Do not vote for the party and do not assume a moral answer. Let the players decide.

  • Released: Norc runs for the woods as soon as he believes he is free. He remembers who spared him.
  • Kept as a guide: he knows the general territory but not Silverlance's lair. He is frightened of the shaman's war band and may bolt if he thinks he can escape.
  • Taken back to Sandpoint: he becomes a prisoner rather than a field guide. Doing so costs time unless the party sends someone else with him.
  • Killed: the information remains true. There is no hidden punishment beyond losing a potentially useful goblin contact.
VTT
Norc should be an NPC token, not a combatant. If the players keep him, move the token with the party into Part II and let his continued survival be an emergent consequence rather than a scheduled plot beat.
6

The Race Begins

The trail now points northeast.

Somewhere in those hills is a wounded unicorn whose lair neither side knows.

Somewhere ahead is a larger goblin war band searching for the same creature.

And Silverlance has already been carrying the cursed arrow since yesterday morning.

The original mission has not disappeared. Mayor Devron still wants the goblin chief dead. But the adventurers now know what the goblins believe can save him, and that puts a living creature between the party and their original target.

Do not tell the players what the "correct" objective is. They may try to save Silverlance, kill him themselves, follow the goblins instead, return to Sandpoint, bargain with Norc, or invent something else. The campaign should follow the decision.

Start the Race Tracker

When the party leaves the clearing for the northeast, begin the three-track procedure in Part II: The Tracker.

Starting state: Party 1 · Goblin war band 1 · Silverlance 10 hp.

The fight at the ford has already consumed part of the day. Do not add a special penalty for it; simply begin the first travel cycle when the adventurers move on.

Possible states going into Part II

  • The party knows the full story and is racing to save Silverlance.
  • The party knows the story but chooses to follow or intercept the goblin war band instead.
  • Norc is travelling with them.
  • Norc is free, dead, or a prisoner in Sandpoint.
  • No goblin survived, and the party is following tracks northeast with only fragments of the truth.

If Silverlance later reaches 0 hp, he dies; that does not automatically cure the goblin chief. His horn remains the objective. Whoever reaches the body first determines what happens to it.

Ends here
Part I ends when the players commit to their next move and the race tracker starts. Continue directly into Part II: The Race for Silverlance if you are not breaking the session.

↑ Contents

Part Two

The Race for Silverlance

An open race · dangerous wilderness · variable encounters · several possible endings

The Charge

What Part Two is for

Part Two turns the search for Silverlance into a visible procedure. The adventurers and the goblin war band are both moving through the same broad stretch of forest without knowing exactly where the unicorn has hidden, while the cursed arrow continues to kill him.

There is no fixed route and no fixed casualty. An orc ambush, a peaceful monster encounter, a death on the trail, or direct contact with the goblin camp are all possible, but none is required. Let the tracker and encounter dice create this group's journey.

GM Snapshot

The adventurers know: Silverlance was wounded by a cursed arrow; the goblin shaman wants his horn; a larger goblin hunt is somewhere northeast; neither side began with the location of the unicorn's lair.

What is actually happening: the goblin shaman is searching the same country from the other side. His war band is cutting timber while it searches. He has built a ridiculous wooden frame of stilts and arm-extenders and is using a spellbook to narrow Silverlance's location.

This part should answer: who makes better progress, what the wilderness costs along the way, and whether the adventurers find Silverlance, the goblin hunt, or a corpse first.

The Discovery Tracker

Two Discovery tracks and one dying unicorn · run one cycle per leg

Discovery is the finish line. Both sides begin at Discovery 1 and are trying to reach Discovery 8. A point of Discovery represents useful ground gained: a correct trail, a ruled-out cave, a landmark recognized, or a stretch of forest successfully eliminated from the search. It is not a literal mile marker.

The Race in One Sentence

Both sides are trying to reach Discovery 8 before Silverlance dies. Each travel cycle, the party navigates and advances, the forest may interfere, the goblins advance, and Silverlance's wound worsens.

Starting State

Adventurers: Discovery 1 of 8 · Goblin war band: Discovery 1 of 8 · Silverlance: 10 hp.

The numbers are an open table mechanic, not information the characters possess with mathematical precision. Put the tracks where everyone can see them and update them in the open.

Cycle Order

  1. Navigation Check. One character leads the leg and rolls under Wisdom on a d20. Apply the result to the party's Discovery track.
  2. Forest Check. Roll 1d6. On 1–3, make a separate Forest Event Roll on the table below. On 4–6, the leg is quiet.
  3. Goblin Progress Roll. Roll 1d6 on the Goblin Progress table and adjust Goblin Discovery.
  4. Wound Roll. Roll 1d6 on Silverlance's Wound table.
  5. Check Discovery. If either side has reached Discovery 8, resolve what it has found. Also resolve direct contact with the war band or Silverlance reaching 0 hp.

1 · Navigation Check

Navigation CheckDiscovery gained
Success+2 Discovery
Failure+1 Discovery
Failure by 5 or more0 Discovery + complication

The party chooses who is actually leading that leg. They may keep the same navigator or change when circumstances change. Do not substitute a particular class or character for the check.

Complication. Roll on the level-one wilderness table in the appendix. A navigation complication gives the encounter the advantage of surprise. If the result can plausibly ambush the party, it receives a free round before initiative. If the result is not naturally hostile, interpret the failed navigation as the party blundering into an awkward position and then use its activity and reaction normally.

2 · Forest Check & Event Roll

Event d6Forest event
1A game trail runs the right way. +1 Party Discovery.
2An abandoned woodcutter's camp offers shelter and a safe place to bind wounds.
3Unicorn sign: dark blood dried on bark at the height of a horse's shoulder. +1 Party Discovery.
4Deadfall, ravines and false trails. −1 Party Discovery, minimum 1.
5The war band's trail crosses the party's route. Reveal the goblins' exact Discovery score and the direction their most recent trail leads.
6Direct contact with the goblin war band. Go to Scene 10: The Enemy Encampment.

Do not repeat results 1–5. Reroll a duplicate or treat the leg as quiet. Result 6 can occur whenever the war band is still active.

3 · Goblin Progress Roll

d6Result
1–2+1 Discovery
3–4+2 Discovery
5–6−1 Discovery, minimum 1

A negative result means the war band spends the leg searching the wrong caves, following bad sign, or doubling back through ground already covered.

4 · Wound Roll

d6Result
1–3−1 hp
4–5No change
6−2 hp

At 0 hp, Silverlance dies. His horn does not teleport into the goblin chief's hands and the chief is not automatically cured. The corpse remains in the meadow. Whoever reaches it first decides what happens to the alicorn.

Time Spent Off the Trail

The campaign already checks encounters by elapsed time. A normal ten-minute binding-wounds break can be folded into the current leg. If the party spends enough extra time resting, hiding, interrogating, or detouring that you would normally make another wilderness encounter check, run a delay cycle without a Navigation Check and without advancing Party Discovery: make the Forest Check, make the Goblin Progress Roll, then make the Wound Roll. Time is the resource this chapter is spending.

The party's camp, a woodcutter's clearing — 24 × 20 · for rests taken during the race

Foundry scene · scene-player-camp.json

7

The Wooded Vale

You head northeast, and by mid-morning the open hills have given way to a wooded vale — old trees, deep shade, and ground softened by years of fallen needles.

Most of it looks untouched. Directly ahead, several trees have been freshly chopped down. The stumps are pale and wet. Yellow chips lie thick around them, and the trunks themselves are gone.

Sight
Axe cuts hacked at bad angles by something short working quickly. The trunks were dragged away rather than trimmed where they fell.
Sound
Birds and insects continue normally. Whoever cut the trees is no longer close enough to disturb the forest.
Smell
Raw sap, sharp and green, over damp needles and old rot.
Feel
Cool air under the canopy and the first real loss of long sight lines in every direction.

Begin the tracker here. Put Party Discovery, Goblin Discovery, and Silverlance's hit points in front of the players before making the first Navigation Check.

The chopped timber is a clue, not an obstacle. The goblins cut these trees. The reason becomes obvious if the party later sees the Stiltwalker: his stilts, arm extenders and wooden frame are all fresh-cut timber. Do not explain the connection for the players.

VTT
Use one simple journey scene with visible counters for Party Discovery, Goblin Discovery and Silverlance. Only change to a tactical map when an actual encounter requires one.
8

Wilderness Encounters

Most groups will not see the same journey. Use the appendix wilderness, activity and reaction tables whenever the procedure calls for a creature encounter. Two ready-to-run encounters are provided below.

Ready Encounter: Orc Ambush

The first warning is a bowstring somewhere among the trees.

Grey-green shapes move between the trunks on both sides of the trail. Some carry bows, others spears and rusted blades. One with a battered shield hangs a step behind the rest and starts barking orders.

Numbers: 2d4 orcs. One is the leader. If this encounter was generated by a navigation complication, the orcs begin split around the party and receive the surprise round.

Orc

Medium humanoid · hit on 14 · 4–6 hp · shortsword, spear or bow 1d6 · XP 9

They use the trees, attack from opposite sides and prefer poorly armored targets when choices are equal. Check morale once half their number is down.

Orc Leader

Medium humanoid · hit on 14 · 6–8 hp · sword and shield · XP 9

The leader stays a pace behind the first rush and gives orders. If the leader falls, make an immediate morale check for the remaining orcs.

No designated victim. Roll or choose targets from the fiction normally. A surprise arrow may kill a hireling, wound a fighter, miss entirely, or create some other disaster. Do not designate a victim in advance.

Orc Ambush on the forest trail — 24 × 30 · cover on both sides of the path

Foundry scene · scene-orc-ambush.json

Ready Encounter: The Beetle Glade

The trees open onto a warm patch of sun. Several beetles the size of large dogs are tumbling over one another in the grass, shells clattering as one tries to climb over another.

They notice you and go still. A faint acrid smell drifts across the glade.

They are watching. They are not yet attacking.

Giant spitting beetles: 1d3. Roll their activity and reaction before deciding what they do. A good reaction leaves them curious or indifferent and allows the party to go around. A hostile reaction brings their caustic spit into play; use the standard Dragonslayer creature statistics.

Avoiding the fight counts. Award the normal encounter experience when the characters successfully handle a dangerous creature without killing it. That policy is worth stating once because it changes how players treat the wilderness.

The Beetle Glade — 22 × 20 · a warm patch of sun the party is allowed to walk around

Foundry scene · scene-beetle-glade.json

GM Principle
A random monster is not automatically a combat encounter. Roll what it is doing and how it reacts. The forest should contain creatures living their own lives, not enemies waiting in initiative order.

The Forest Ruin — 22 × 20 · a spare wilderness site for a rolled encounter or a night's shelter

Foundry scene · scene-forest-ruin.json

9

Resolving the Race

The Discovery tracker is allowed to change the next chapter. Do not force a tie or steer the numbers toward a preferred result.

If the adventurers reach Discovery 8 first

They find the final signs leading toward Silverlance's meadow before the goblin shaman does. If they are searching for the unicorn, they may press directly toward the Meadow of Oaks. Goblin Discovery remains active unless the party has already neutralized, diverted or bargained with the war band.

If the party's declared objective was to find the war band rather than Silverlance, Discovery 8 instead means they locate its encampment. Go to Scene 10.

If the goblins reach Discovery 8 first

The Stiltwalker reaches Discovery 8 and fixes Silverlance's location. The scattered war band abruptly stops checking caves, reforms, and begins moving with purpose. The adventurers can follow the concentrated trail, attempt to overtake it, or abandon the pursuit. Record that the goblins know where they are going; do not instantly give them Silverlance's horn.

If both sides reach Discovery 8 in the same cycle

Both sides reach the answer during the same cycle and converge on the same part of the forest. This can become a three-way arrival at Silverlance's meadow, a stalking encounter just outside it, or an attempt by one side to ambush the other. Preserve the current Silverlance hit-point total and let positioning decide the rest.

If Silverlance reaches 0 hp first

He dies from the cursed wound. The race continues, but its object changes from rescue to possession of the horn. A party that arrives first finds the dead unicorn and can protect, hide, destroy or take the alicorn. Goblins who arrive first can attempt to remove it and carry it back to the chief.

If the party encounters the war band before Discovery 8

Go to Scene 10. The race has not magically ended. The characters have simply found the rival hunting party before either side has found Silverlance.

10

The Enemy Encampment

Through the trees, close enough now to hear clearly, a goblin war band is throwing together a camp in a hurry. Tent poles lean at bad angles. A cauldron hangs over a fire. Fresh-cut wood is stacked beside half-finished frames.

One goblin is larger and better armed than the rest, barking orders while the others work.

But the strangest figure is at the far edge of the camp.

It is a goblin standing on wooden stilts with wooden extenders strapped along its arms, making a creature barely four feet tall loom more than six feet high. Filthy furs are lashed across the frame. A pumpkin has been hollowed out and worn as a helmet.

The Stiltwalker holds an open book in both extended hands. He is not watching his camp. He is reading aloud and staring into the forest in one very particular direction.

Sight
A temporary camp, not a fortification. Fresh-cut firewood, half-raised shelters, rusted weapons and one much better axe in the hands of the champion.
Sound
Chopping, arguing, tent poles knocking together. Beneath it all, the shaman's steady reading in a language that makes the air feel tight.
Smell
Woodsmoke, rancid fur, cooking meat and the same sharp cut-pine smell as the stumps in Scene 7.
Feel
Damp ground under the undergrowth and the sudden realization that the party has found the hunters rather than their quarry.

What the shaman is doing. He is trying to locate Silverlance. The war band has spent days checking likely caves and gullies. If Goblin Discovery reaches 8, the reading succeeds and the band starts moving directly toward the meadow.

The Stiltwalker is the important target. The camp's numbers are dangerous, but killing, distracting, robbing or otherwise stopping the shaman can prevent further Goblin Discovery even if most of the war band survives. Let the players discover that from what he is doing rather than announcing an objective marker.

The wood pays off here. His stilts, arm extenders and frame are built from the freshly felled timber the party saw upon entering the vale.

If Norc is with the party, he recognizes the shaman and the goblin champion and can identify which one actually leads the hunt. He does not automatically start a mutiny or make a deal simply because that happened in another campaign.

Do not roll initiative yet. The party may observe, withdraw, creep closer, attack, sabotage the camp, attempt to steal the spellbook, follow the shaman's gaze, call out, wait for darkness, or invent something better. Their decision is the opening situation of Part III.

The Stiltwalker's Camp — 26 × 24 · Scene 10 and the whole of Part Three

Foundry scene · scene-stiltwalkers-camp.json

VTT
Have the camp map ready but begin with the party outside it and the goblins unaware unless the approach says otherwise. Place the cauldron, firewood stack, unfinished tents and Stiltwalker visibly; all are actionable terrain, not decoration.

End of Part Two

Record the state, not a canonical result

Part Two ends when the race produces a decisive contact: the adventurers find the goblin hunt, one side identifies Silverlance's location, both sides converge, or the unicorn dies.

RecordCarry forward
Party DiscoveryThe current score and what objective the party was pursuing.
Goblin DiscoveryThe current score; retire it only if the war band abandons or loses the hunt.
SilverlanceCurrent hp, or dead. Never reset him between sessions.
NorcWith the party, free, imprisoned, missing, or dead.
Casualties & resourcesWho actually died, current hit points, broken gear, spells, rations and hirelings.
What the party foundSilverlance's trail, the enemy camp, the Stiltwalker's purpose, or some combination.

There is deliberately no “standing at the end of Part Two” diagram. Whatever numbers are on your table are the correct numbers.

↑ Contents

Part Three

The Stiltwalker's Camp

A branching confrontation · a possible coup · the mist · and Silverlance's meadow

The Charge

What Part Three is for

Part Three resolves the crisis created by the race. The adventurers have finally reached either the goblin hunt, Silverlance's trail, or the unicorn himself. From here the campaign stops being a search and becomes a choice: what happens to the Stiltwalker, what happens to Silverlance, and who will rule the goblins when the current chief is gone?

Do not force the four scenes into a fixed order. A party that found the camp first may fight or bargain there before reaching the meadow. A party that found Silverlance first may save him and deal with the Stiltwalker afterward. If the goblins won the race, the confrontation may happen on the move or at the edge of the meadow. If Silverlance is already dead, the object of the struggle is his horn.

GM Snapshot

The adventurers know: the goblin chief is dying; the shaman believes Silverlance's alicorn can cure him; the Stiltwalker is directing the hunt; and the unicorn may have very little time left.

What is actually happening: the Stiltwalker has nearly completed his search. His book and marked search papers contain two useful pieces of information: the route to Silverlance's meadow and the location of the goblin chief's cave. Norc may see the crisis as his chance to replace the chief, but he is not required for the adventure to continue.

This part should answer: whether Silverlance lives, whether the goblins obtain his horn, what becomes of the Stiltwalker and his war band, and how the adventurers learn where the chief is.

Starting Part Three

Begin from the state Part Two actually produced

End of Part TwoBegin here
The adventurers found the enemy campBegin with Scene 11: The Cooking Fires. The goblins are unaware unless the party exposed itself.
The adventurers found Silverlance firstGo to Scene 14: The Meadow of Oaks. The goblin search remains active unless already broken.
The goblins found Silverlance's trail firstThe camp is being struck. The Stiltwalker leads the war band toward the meadow. The party may shadow, overtake, ambush, or race them there.
Both sides convergedPut both groups near the meadow and let scouting and positioning determine who sees whom first.
Silverlance diedGo to the meadow when either side reaches it, but use the Silverlance is dead result in Scene 14. The race is now for possession of the alicorn.

Norc's state matters only when it should. If he is alive, free, and on terms with the party, he can become a powerful complication in Scene 12. If he is dead, imprisoned, hostile, or simply elsewhere, nothing breaks. The Stiltwalker's papers and surviving goblins can carry the information the campaign needs.

Scene Key

Four situations · use only the ones play reaches

11

The Cooking Fires

Woodsmoke drifts between the trees before the camp itself comes into view. Goblins are chopping, arguing, hauling firewood and trying to raise crooked shelters around a boiling cauldron.

One larger goblin carries a hand axe too good for the rest of the band and shouts orders from beside the fire.

At the far edge stands the Stiltwalker: a goblin made absurdly tall by wooden legs and arm-frames, filthy furs hanging from the whole contraption, a hollow pumpkin over his head. An open book rests in his extended hands.

He is reading. He is staring past the camp into the trees. He is not paying attention to anything behind him.

Sight
A firewood stack tall enough to fight from, a full cauldron, half-raised tents, crude weapons, and rolls of marked hide and parchment near the shaman's packs.
Sound
Axes, bickering, iron pots, tent poles and the Stiltwalker's low recitation underneath it all.
Smell
Meat, woodsmoke, rancid fur and fresh-cut pine — the same sharp smell as the missing trees in the vale.
Feel
Wet ground under the brush and the rare advantage of finding an enemy camp that is busy doing everything except keeping watch.

If the camp is still occupied

Reward an unseen approach. The distracted camp is normally surprised on 1–2; if the characters approach quietly while the goblins are cooking, chopping and arguing, increase that to 1–4. Tell the players what earned the advantage. If they announce themselves, attack from the open, or arrive after the Stiltwalker has ordered the camp broken, use normal surprise instead.

Use the terrain. The firewood gives high ground (+1 to hit). The cauldron can be tipped or thrown if someone can get to it. The fire can ignite tents and dry gear. The Stiltwalker's wooden frame is awkward in dense brush. None of this requires a prescribed stunt.

The Stiltwalker's entangle

When seriously threatened, the shaman raises the book and causes the grass and roots across the center of the camp to surge upward. The spell is deliberately indiscriminate: goblins and adventurers are caught alike.

  • Everyone in the area makes the appropriate save.
  • Failure means immobilized until freed or the spell ends.
  • Success allows movement at half speed through the growth.
  • Entangled creatures are attacked at +4.

The spell should change the geometry of the fight, not merely add a condition marker. Goblins curse their own shaman when vines catch them. Fighters hack lanes through the growth. The fire becomes dangerous. A retreat that looked impossible may suddenly be open.

The cauldron

If the players try to weaponize the boiling cauldron, use the campaign's improvisation rule rather than requiring any particular solution. A good baseline is a Strength check to overturn or redirect it and a save versus breath weapon for anyone caught in the spill. On a failed save, 2d6 scalding damage is appropriate; a badly burned survivor attacks at −4 until the end of the fight. Charge 1 point of damage only if the character actually grabs or braces against the hot iron.

Goblin War-Band Fighter

Small humanoid · target to hit 14 before bonuses · 4–7 hp · hand axe or spear 1d6 · morale 7 · XP 7

Use as many as actually remain in the war band. They seek flanks, exploit entangled targets, and check morale once half the fighting goblins are down.

Goblin Champion

Small humanoid · target to hit 14 before bonuses · recommended 8 hp · attack +2 · good hand axe 1d6+1 · morale 9

These values make the champion the obvious physical threat beneath the shaman. If he falls, make an immediate morale check for ordinary goblins who are not already committed to Norc.

The Stiltwalker

Goblin shaman on wooden stilts · recommended target to hit 14 · recommended 7 hp · club 1d6 · spellcaster

His known magic includes the mass entangle above and cause light wounds: save versus spells or suffer 1d8+1 damage from black unholy fire.

Tactics: he uses entangle to break a rush, then punishes whichever enemy has hurt him or the champion most. He is proud enough to fight when escape would be wiser.

The search materials

Beside the Stiltwalker's bedroll are his book, charcoal notes and a crude map marked with two places. One mark identifies the Meadow of Oaks; the other marks the cave of the goblin chief. The writing is crude and partly magical, but the landmarks are clear enough to follow.

If the party obtains these materials before finding Silverlance, grant +3 Party Discovery, capped at 8. If the race is already resolved, the papers simply give the direct route to the meadow and the location needed to begin Part IV.

VTT
Keep the cauldron, fire, stacked wood, tents, shaman's book and search papers visible and interactable. Start the party outside the camp unless their previous choices put them somewhere else. Do not start initiative until somebody commits to violence.
12

Norc's Choice

Use only if Norc is alive and the situation gives him a reason to act

Norc is not scripted to rescue the party. He is a goblin with an opportunity.

If Norc was freed earlier

He has had time to find two dissatisfied goblins who would rather back a new chief than die for a shaman's desperate hunt. They may appear during the camp confrontation, shadow the party beforehand, or approach after the Stiltwalker is weakened. Their timing should follow what Norc knows, not what the fight needs.

If Norc is travelling with the party

He recognizes the champion, the shaman and the political weakness of the war band. Before a fight he can propose treachery outright. During one, he may turn if he believes the Stiltwalker can actually be killed.

If Norc is dead, hostile or absent

Skip this scene. A defeated war band can still surrender, flee or splinter through ordinary morale and reaction rolls. The search materials still lead to Silverlance and the chief.

The offer

Norc looks from the dead and wounded goblins to the Stiltwalker's papers, then back at you.

"Old chief sick. Old chief die. Norc can be chief."

He points toward the forest.

"You no kill Norc. Norc help find white horse. You help Norc take cave. Then Sandpoint no get raid from Norc goblins."

The bargain is simple: Norc helps end the hunt and gives the party the route to the chief; the adventurers remove the current chief and leave Norc a chance to claim the tribe.

He is sincere about wanting the throne and sincere that peace with Sandpoint would benefit him. That does not make the future promise guaranteed. Do not require the players to accept him merely because the bargain is useful.

If the coup happens during combat

Norc and his supporters attack the Stiltwalker or champion from the goblin side. Immediately check morale for ordinary goblins who witness it. Some may flee, some may join Norc, and some may keep fighting. Do not predetermine which two surviving goblins die on the way out.

After the camp

If Norc controls the survivors, he orders the hunt for Silverlance ended. He will not willingly enter the unicorn's meadow. He and his followers remain at or near the camp while the adventurers go on, unless the party has negotiated something different.

Fried rats: the goblins have a bag of cooked rats among their food. Anyone desperate enough to eat one recovers 1d3 hp. They are edible, greasy and revolting. Nobody is required to know that in advance; inspecting or identifying them is enough.

Spoils of the camp

  • 30 sp among pouches and cook gear.
  • The champion's good hand axe, if he is defeated or disarmed.
  • The Stiltwalker's club (1d6), if recovered.
  • The Stiltwalker's spellbook, containing at least entangle and cause light wounds.
  • Frogman gear: mask, fins and a small reusable air bladder providing roughly four rounds of underwater breathing. It looks ridiculous here and may become extremely useful later.

Award normal encounter experience for enemies defeated, routed, captured or otherwise overcome.

GM Principle
Norc is a consequence of mercy, not a mandatory ally. If the players created a relationship with him, pay it off. If they did not, do not force him back into the story merely because he would be convenient.
13

The Mist

The trees ahead pale behind a wall of white. Within minutes the forest has become trunks standing in a cold blank room, each one appearing only when you are almost close enough to touch it.

Sound comes from the wrong direction. Water beads on weapons and mail. The trail that seemed obvious ten minutes ago has vanished.

Then somebody notices the same fallen log for the second time.

Sight
Twenty feet of visibility at best. Beyond that, silhouettes become whatever the imagination needs them to be.
Sound
Muffled footsteps, close voices and distant noises that seem to come from directly behind the party.
Smell
Cold water, wet bark and almost nothing else.
Feel
Condensation on skin and armor, and the pressure of knowing that delay still matters if Silverlance is alive.

Run this as a group Wisdom check. Every character actively helping to navigate rolls. Hirelings may roll if the party actually entrusts them with the route. A majority of successes gets the group through cleanly.

  • Majority succeeds: the party reaches the Meadow of Oaks without losing meaningful time.
  • Majority fails: the party circles back and loses time. If Silverlance is still dying, make one additional wound-decline roll before they arrive.
  • Tie: the party must choose which navigator to trust. That character makes one final Wisdom check. Failure costs the same extra time.

If the party has the Stiltwalker's map, it prevents them from leaving the correct region but does not make the mist disappear. If they have no map and no surviving guide, a failed group check may also trigger a normal wilderness encounter before another attempt.

VTT
This does not need a tactical map. Put the group check in the open, keep Silverlance's current hp visible if he is alive, and let the table feel what one wasted leg could cost.
14

The Meadow of Oaks

The mist thins into a quiet meadow ringed by enormous oaks. The grass is flattened beneath one of them.

A white, horse-like creature lies there with an ivory horn rising from its brow and a short white beard beneath its jaw. Blood mats one side of its body. The broken shaft of an arrow stands out from the wound near its spine.

If this is Silverlance, the stories left out how large he is.

Sight
The arrow has snapped off short. The grass around Silverlance is crushed from repeated attempts to rise.
Sound
Very few birds. If he lives, his breathing is fast and sometimes stops for a frightening second before beginning again.
Smell
Crushed grass, old blood and a faint scorched-metal odor around the cursed wound.
Feel
A place that seems calm without being safe. Even badly wounded, a unicorn is a large frightened animal with a horn like a spear.

The Meadow of Oaks — 24 × 22 · a quiet objective first, a battle map only if the goblins arrive

Foundry scene · scene-meadow-of-oaks.json

If Silverlance is alive

Approach is primarily a trust problem. A good-aligned divine character or someone who has clearly acted to protect the meadow may approach without a roll. Others can earn trust through a calm approach, lowered weapons, healing magic, food, or a successful Charisma check. A failed roll does not make Silverlance attack on command; it means he will not allow that character close enough to touch the arrow yet.

Removing the cursed arrow. Once somebody is trusted close enough, call for a Wisdom check to draw it safely. Appropriate healing magic or a particularly careful plan may grant +4 or remove the need for the roll. On failure Silverlance recoils and the arrow remains; another attempt requires a changed approach, and if time is still being tracked make another wound-decline roll before it.

On success, the hand around the wound takes on a faint warm light. The black shaft comes free. The wound closes behind it, slowly at first and then all at once. When the arrow hits the grass it sizzles and smokes.

Silverlance gets one foreleg beneath himself, then the other. Light gathers along his coat and horn until the meadow seems brighter than the sky above it.

The light passes through you like warm water.

Every bruise, cut and puncture closes.

Then a voice that does not come through your ears says one thing:

Thank you.

Silverlance's blessing: every living creature in the meadow is restored to full hit points and relieved of ordinary wounds. This is intentionally generous. The race has been punishing; saving the unicorn is the release.

Talking with him: Silverlance communicates telepathically and briefly. He can confirm that the arrow was cursed and that goblins hunted him, but he does not know the politics of their tribe. He will not bargain over his horn and will not accompany the party to exterminate goblins. Keep him ancient, wary and economical with words.

Reward for saving Silverlance

Award 650 XP. In addition, roll once on the module's mundane treasure table for each adventurer who took part in the rescue. If you want the rescue to feel especially fairy-tale and strange, make one additional roll on the weird-item table for the whole party.

If Silverlance is dead when the party arrives

The meadow is silent. The arrow is still lodged in the corpse unless someone has already removed it, and the alicorn remains attached unless the goblins reached him first.

  • Party first: they decide whether to guard, hide, remove, destroy or carry the horn. There is no healing burst and no 650 XP rescue award.
  • Goblins first: the Stiltwalker or surviving hunters attempt to remove the horn and carry it to the chief. Track who actually has it; do not declare the chief cured until the horn reaches him and the shaman's cure is attempted.
  • Both sides arrive: run the meadow as a three-way objective fight. The corpse is terrain and the horn is the prize.

If the goblins arrive while Silverlance still lives

Do not freeze the unicorn while the two humanoid groups fight around him. He is wounded, frightened and dangerous. If threatened directly he kicks, charges or tries to flee as his remaining strength allows. Characters who protect rather than merely possess him should have an easier time earning his trust afterward.

The cursed arrow

If recovered, the arrow is physical evidence that somebody armed the goblins with magic beyond their normal means. It continues to smell of scorched metal and should be treated as dangerous until identified.

VTT
Use the meadow as a quiet objective map first and a battle map only if another group arrives. Keep Silverlance's current hp exactly where Part II left it. If he was already saved earlier, use this scene only for the conversation, blessing and consequences that have not yet occurred.

Ending Part Three

Carry the result into the Cave of the Goblin King

Part Three ends when the immediate struggle over Silverlance is resolved and the adventurers know where the goblin chief can be found. Record the state rather than forcing a predetermined outcome.

RecordPossible states
SilverlanceHealed, alive but still wounded, dead with horn intact, or dead with horn taken.
AlicornOn Silverlance, protected by the party, in goblin hands, hidden, destroyed, or otherwise accounted for.
The StiltwalkerDead, captured, fled, allied by some unlikely bargain, or still hunting.
NorcPotential claimant, party ally of convenience, prisoner, rival, absent, or dead.
Goblin war bandDestroyed, routed, split by mutiny, serving Norc, still loyal to the shaman, or scattered.
Route to the chiefFrom the Stiltwalker's map, Norc, interrogation, tracking retreating goblins, or another solution earned in play.

Part IV changes with these answers. A healed Silverlance may make his meadow safe enough to rest in. A dead Silverlance removes that protection. Norc may offer help, or may already be maneuvering for the throne. If the goblins carried the horn home, the chief may be in the process of being cured when the adventurers reach the cave.

There is no canonical camp massacre, no required mutiny, no required goblin alliance, and no guaranteed unicorn rescue. Whatever happened at your table is now the campaign.

↑ Contents

Part Four

The Cave of the Goblin King

Approach to the chief’s cave · four keyed areas · an older shrine beneath goblin occupation

The Charge

What Part Four is for

The adventurers finally know where the goblin chief is hiding. Their original commission can now be completed — if they can get through the tribe around him.

The first surprise is that this is not merely a goblin cave. Behind the rough entrance are worked stone, proper doors, a rune-carved fountain and a consecrated altar. The goblins are occupying something much older than their tribe and have vandalized pieces they do not understand. Do not explain who built it. The dungeon itself is the clue.

Part Four should establish three things: the condition of the goblin defenses, the existence of the older complex beneath them, and the two ways deeper into the cave. It should not assume Silverlance survived, Norc became an ally, or any particular character class is present.

GM Snapshot

The adventurers know: the goblin chief is somewhere inside this cave. Depending on Part Three, they may also know that the chief is dying, that the Stiltwalker sought Silverlance's horn as a cure, and that Norc wants the throne for himself.

What is actually happening: the cave mouth and nearby living spaces belong to the goblins, but the worked chambers beyond them predate the tribe. A large concentration of goblins lies beyond the northwest passage from the fountain. The eastern route leads through the altar and into a web-choked side of the complex.

This part should answer: how alert the cave is, what the adventurers learn about the place beneath the goblin occupation, and which route they choose deeper into the complex.

Before the Cave

Carry forward what Part Three actually produced

Do not reset the board between chapters. Use the state recorded at the end of Part Three.

Part Three resultEffect here
Silverlance survived and was savedThe party may rest in his meadow if they choose. His healing has already happened; do not grant it a second time. The meadow is protected enough that overnight encounter checks occur only on a 1 on d6.
Silverlance diedThere is no protected recovery unless the party found another safe place. Camp and encounter checks work normally.
The Stiltwalker or goblin hunters escapedIncrease the Cave Alert by one step. Survivors have had time to warn the chief's people.
Goblins escaped with Silverlance's alicornIncrease Cave Alert by one step and record that the horn may already be inside. Do not decide the chief's final condition yet; carry the horn and Stiltwalker's status forward to the later confrontation.
Norc is allied with the partyHe wants the chief dead, but he also wants to inherit the tribe. He normally waits outside with any followers rather than be seen marching beside outsiders. The party can bargain with him to do otherwise.
Norc is hostile, dead, imprisoned or absentNothing breaks. The party has the route from the Stiltwalker's papers, another captured goblin, or its own tracking.

Cave Alert

123

Start at 1 — Complacent unless the results above increase it. The maximum is 3.

  1. Complacent. Two drunken sentries occupy Area 1. They expect no attack.
  2. Wary. The two sentries are sober and another pair is close enough to join after the first round unless stopped.
  3. Alarmed. Four armed goblins hold Area 1, the moss curtain is watched from within, and deeper goblins know intruders may be coming.

Increase Alert during play when survivors escape deeper into the cave, a loud fight continues for several rounds, or the party deliberately raises an alarm. Quiet kills, deception and careful exploration can preserve the current state.

Reaching the entrance

From the Stiltwalker's camp or Silverlance's meadow, the marked route reaches the cave in roughly twenty minutes. If you are using ten-minute dungeon and wilderness turns, make two encounter checks on the approach. Do not predeclare them clear.

The forest grows rougher as the party closes in: fresh stumps, muddy boot prints, crude trail marks and finally a dirt path climbing into high wooded hills. The cave mouth itself is hidden behind a thick hanging curtain of moss.

Outside the Goblin Cave — 26 × 24 · the approach and the moss curtain

Foundry scene · scene-outside-the-cave.json

Map of the Cave

Tap an area to jump to its entry · a fresh key, numbered from one

✧ fountain▲ altar▨ webbing▬ door– – unexplored1 sq = 5 ft.

Worked stone beneath goblin squalor — this complex is older than its current occupants

Area Key

Four areas · two routes deeper into the cave

1

The Guard Hollow

A curtain of heavy green moss hangs across the cave mouth from stone above to mud below. Boot prints disappear beneath it in both directions.

Beyond the moss comes the smell of stale ale, woodsmoke and old straw. Voices echo somewhere farther inside.

Sight
Moss thick enough to hide the entrance completely. Heavy goblin traffic has flattened the earth around it.
Sound
Muted voices inside. At Alert 1, occasional drunken laughter. At Alert 2 or 3, the entrance is noticeably quieter.
Smell
Sour ale, old straw, smoke and the mineral cold of a cave breathing outward.
Feel
Wet moss dragging across skin and equipment like a curtain of hanging rope.

Watching the entrance

If the adventurers observe instead of entering immediately, the normal guard routine becomes obvious. At Alert 1, one drunken sentry steps outside every few minutes with a tankard, makes a lazy show of looking around and returns inside. At Alert 2, the sentries take turns outside without drinking. At Alert 3, nobody exposes himself without another goblin covering the moss curtain from within.

A scout can approach the entrance using the normal stealth rules. Roll thief stealth behind the screen if that is your table's practice. On failure, reveal the failure through the fiction — a snapped branch, dislodged stone or rustle of brush — rather than by announcing the number.

Goblin Cave Sentry

Small humanoid · target to hit 14 before bonuses · 4–7 hp · hand axe 1d6 · morale 7 · XP 7

At Alert 1 they are drunk and inattentive: −4 on their first attack or perception-related check after being surprised. At Alert 2 or 3 use normal statistics. Check morale once half the sentries are down.

Inside the hollow

The chamber has a low ceiling, two straw sleeping mats, a heap of fresh straw thrown over older bedding and a battered locked chest. A passage climbs from here to a wooden door leading to Area 2.

The chest: the lock can be picked normally. A character examining it notices that it is brittle with rust; brute force can open it with an appropriate Strength check or crowbar, but a failed attempt mangles the lock and costs another dungeon turn.
