The rusty key is hidden in one of the sleeping mats and is found automatically by anyone who thoroughly searches the straw.

Inside: 18 gp, a small ruby worth 50 gp, and a potion of superheroism. Each of the two regular sentries carries exactly 1 gp. The neat total of twenty gold pieces looks more like a payment than scavenged goblin treasure. Reinforcements added by a higher Alert state carry only ordinary small change.

GM: the twenty gold came from the young black dragon's small hoard. The sentries do not know that. They only know that guarding this entrance suddenly started paying very well.

The potion: identify it using the campaign's normal potion rules, including the small-sip method if that house rule is in play. Apply the normal Dragonslayer restrictions on who can benefit from superheroism.

VTT
Place the moss curtain as a vision blocker that can be crossed. Keep sentries inside until observation, stealth or noise determines their positions. Do not start combat merely because the party reaches the entrance.
2

The Fountain of Destna

The wooden door opens on shimmering golden light, moving over the walls and ceiling like sunlight reflected from water.

A stone fountain stands in the center of the chamber, covered in careful runes. Goblins have hacked crude marks and broken Common across parts of the carving, but they have not managed to destroy it.

This room was built. Properly built. Worked stone replaces the rough cave walls, and a good door leads east. A second, rougher passage runs northwest.

Sight
Golden light rippling across worked stone. Goblin graffiti cut over older runes. Water that remains perfectly clear despite the occupation around it.
Sound
Running water. Anyone who stops to listen can make out numerous muffled goblin voices from the northwest passage.
Smell
Wet stone and a faint metallic sweetness. The usual goblin stink is strangely absent from this chamber.
Feel
Cool spray on skin. The unmistakable sense that this room belongs to a different place and a different age than the cave outside it.

The inscription

An Intelligence check deciphers enough of the damaged runes to understand the promise: Offer gold to Destna, Lady of Fortune, and drink of her water to receive her favor.

Anyone may refuse without penalty. A character who drops at least one gold piece into the fountain and drinks rolls once on the table below. Each creature can receive only one blessing from this fountain during the adventure.

d10Destna's blessing
1–3Fortune's Nudge. +1 to the character's next attack roll, saving throw or ability check; the blessing ends after it is used.
4–5Sure Step. +2 to one saving throw or ability check made before the end of the next combat. The player may declare it before rolling.
6–7Golden Guard. +1 Armor Class through the end of the next combat.
8–9Destna's Shield. +2 Armor Class through the end of the next combat.
10Great Favor. Choose attacks, saving throws or Armor Class. Gain +2 to the chosen category until the end of this expedition into the cave.

A blessed character glows softly gold for a few heartbeats, making the result visibly supernatural.

Two routes

Northwest: the rough passage carries the sound of many goblins. This route leads toward the tribe's occupied heart and is still unexplored in this part.

East: a proper wooden door opens toward Area 3 and the older shrine rooms.

Do not have an NPC choose for the party. The sound from the northwest is enough information for the players to decide whether they want the direct goblin route or the quieter worked-stone route.

VTT
Keep the golden light and northwest audio cue obvious. The fountain is an offer, not a trick. Roll blessings openly and record them beside the affected token so they are not forgotten later.
3

The Altar of Humility

Red light fills this chamber.

Two stone statues stand on opposite sides of a dusty altar carved with runes. A large red gemstone cut in the shape of a heart rests on the altar, glowing from within.

Bones lie scattered across the floor — goblin and human both.

Then a voice rolls out of the stonework:

“Approach with humility and live.”

A heavy padlocked door waits in the south wall.

Sight
The statues' mouths are open and blackened with soot. Bones nearest the altar are relatively intact; those lying in front of the statues are scorched and fragmented.
Sound
The warning seems to come from the room itself. Afterward there is only silence.
Smell
Old ash, scorched bone and dust.
Feel
Red light without heat. Grit and small bone fragments underfoot.

The warning is literal

The statues project sheets of flame across the approach to the altar at roughly chest height. A creature that advances upright into the trapped zone triggers them: 2d6 fire damage, save versus breath weapon for half. The statues can fire again on a later attempt; they are not single-use traps.

Kneeling, crawling or otherwise approaching below the statues' line of fire is safe. Once a character reaches the altar itself, standing there does not trigger the flames. The room says exactly what it means.

Careful examination reveals the soot-black mouths and the consistent height of the scorch marks without a roll. An Intelligence check may connect those clues to the word humility, but never require the check if the players solve it themselves.

Tampering with the statues

A thief or similarly equipped character can try to disable a statue. Use the character's normal trap-disarming chance. If your campaign uses the backfire house rule, a result of 81–100 triggers the statue immediately in addition to failing. Each statue must be disabled separately.

The important point is that disarming is optional. Clever movement is the intended safe answer.

The Energy Heart

When lifted from the altar, the gemstone shrinks to palm size and the red illumination dies, leaving the room dark unless the party has another light source.

Energy Heart: once per day, when its bearer would take fire, acid, cold or electrical damage, the heart can absorb 10 points of that damage. Excess damage still affects the bearer normally.

Removing the heart does not deactivate the statues. The warning and their firing mechanism remain in force on the return trip.

The south door

The heavy padlock can be picked normally or broken with tools and an appropriate Strength check. Smashing it is loud enough to increase Cave Alert by one step if the cave is not already Alarmed. Beyond is Area 4.

VTT
Show the statue mouths, soot and floor bones. Do not hide the physical clues behind perception rolls. Set the flame lanes as templates so players can understand what they have learned after the first trigger—or avoid triggering them at all.
4

The Web Room

Thick webs hang from every corner and sag across the ceiling in grey ropes. Hundreds of tiny spiders move through them.

Every one of those spiders is far too small to have spun webbing this heavy.

A goblin corpse hangs cocooned against one wall. Beyond it, a rough passage continues northeast into darkness.

Sight
Webbing strong enough to hold a body upright. The cocooned goblin has several deep punctures through the wrapping.
Sound
A dry rustle of thousands of tiny legs overhead. Occasionally a heavier strand gives a slow creak.
Smell
Dust, dry rot and the sweet smell of something dead inside silk.
Feel
Webbing catches on packs, armor and weapon hilts. Moving quietly through the room is difficult.

The ambush

Three baby giant black widows cling motionless above the room. They do not automatically gain surprise. When the first adventurer moves beneath the central webbing or begins disturbing the corpse, roll surprise using the campaign's d4 ambush-predator rule. On a successful surprise result, place the spiders inside or immediately adjacent to the party's formation before resolving their attacks.

Characters who explicitly study the ceiling, burn away webbing from a distance, send an animal ahead or devise another sensible precaution can deny the spiders their surprise roll. Reward the warning signs.

Baby Giant Black Widow

Large spider · 1 HD each (roll hp individually) · bite 1d4 · fast climber · ambush predator

Paralyzing bite: a creature damaged by the bite saves versus poison. On a failure it is paralyzed for the duration you normally use for a lesser giant-spider venom; the young spiders do not possess the adult widow's lethal poison.

Tactics: roll or choose targets without sophisticated coordination. They drop, bite and retreat into webbing when badly hurt. They are animals defending a feeding ground, not goblin allies.

For a fixed spread, give the three spiders 4, 5 and 8 hp. Otherwise roll each 1 HD creature openly when the ambush begins.

The cocooned goblin

Once the spiders are dealt with—or if the party can reach it safely—the corpse can be cut down and searched. It carries:

  • 14 gp in a tied pouch.
  • A finely carved wooden dragon toy, worth about 50 gp.
  • A wand of magic missiles.

The dragon toy is a clue before it is treasure. Do not explain why a dead goblin in this cave was carrying it.

The northeast passage

The rough passage continues toward Area 5. Air coming from that direction is colder and wetter than the rooms behind the party. The web room itself provides no reason they must continue immediately; retreat, healing and reconsideration remain valid choices.

VTT
Place the three spiders on the ceiling layer or keep them hidden until their ambush is resolved. The cocooned corpse should be visible from the entrance. If surprise succeeds, drop the spider tokens among the party rather than lining them politely across the far side of the room.

Ending Part Four

The cave has become something larger than the job

Part Four ends naturally when the adventurers have explored these first worked chambers and decide whether to continue northeast toward Area 5, return to the fountain and take the northwest route toward the goblins, or withdraw.

Record Cave Alert, which sentries escaped, which blessings remain active, whether the Energy Heart was taken, and whether the party has discovered the wand and dragon toy. Those facts belong to the table now and carry forward unchanged.

↑ Contents

Part Five

The Pillar and the Pool

Area 5 · an optional shortcut · a baited pool · something watching from the dark

The Charge

What Part Five is for

Part Five reveals that the goblins are not the strangest thing living in this complex.

The eastern branch beyond the web room opens into a vast flooded cavern built around a rune-covered obelisk. A small island glitters across the water, an eastern passage continues beyond it, and something beneath the surface is waiting for swimmers. High above, a young black dragon has been watching the goblins, the pool and now the adventurers.

Nothing in this chamber is required to reach the goblin chief. The party can withdraw to the Fountain of Destna and take the northwest passage toward Area 6. Crossing the pool instead offers a dangerous shortcut and the chance to learn that a much larger threat is present.

GM Snapshot

The adventurers know: numerous goblin voices lie somewhere beyond the older complex. They may already suspect that the goblins are occupying rather than building these chambers.

What is actually happening: the island's glittering "hoard" is worthless bait. A grasping aquatic growth waits beneath the water for creatures that swim toward it. The obelisk can temporarily quiet the hazard if its runes are understood. A young black dragon rests high in the cavern and studies anyone who enters.

This part should reveal: that the flooded chamber is a deliberate trap, that the ancient complex had means of controlling it, and—if the party lingers—that a dragon is involved in whatever is happening here.

Map of the Pillar Cavern

Area 5 · crossing the pool is optional

≋ water✦ bait△ loose scree▮ obelisk1 sq = 5 ft.

The shortest way forward is not necessarily the safest

5

The Pillar Cavern

The corridor opens into a cavern so large your light cannot find the roof. Near the shore stands a stone obelisk taller than a man, every face crowded with faintly glowing glyphs.

Most of the cavern floor is water: a wide, absolutely still pool that swallows the light a few yards from shore. A small island rises from the middle of it, heaped with something that glitters like coins and jewels.

Beyond the pool, an opening in the eastern wall leads on into darkness. From somewhere past it come the muffled voices of many goblins.

Sight
One image dominates the obelisk's carvings: waves. The glitter on the island is bright enough to catch the eye immediately. The water itself is unnaturally flat.
Sound
Muffled goblin voices beyond the far passage. No dripping and almost no lapping from the pool, despite the size of the cavern.
Smell
Cold mineral water and wet stone. Nothing decays here.
Feel
Cold rolls off the water. The scree along both sides shifts under even a cautious boot and slides toward the pool.

The choice

The far passage eventually reconnects with the goblin-held route toward Area 6, but the pool blocks the direct way. The steep edges to either side are loose, collapsing scree and cannot be crossed on foot.

The party does not have to cross. They can return through Areas 4 and 2 and take the northwest passage toward the goblin voices. Crossing the pool is faster and puts the glittering island within reach, but it exposes them to the thing beneath the water.

The obelisk

The source of the runes is older than the goblin occupation. Anyone examining them for a dungeon turn can attempt an Intelligence check. A character with relevant magical, scholarly or religious knowledge may receive whatever bonus you normally grant for applicable expertise.

Success: the repeated wave glyph is not a label but a command. Pressing the largest wave symbol makes the pool ripple outward from the obelisk and causes the grasping growth beneath the water to curl tightly against the bottom for one turn. During that time the pool can be crossed without attack from it.

Failure: the character recognizes that the glyphs concern the pool but cannot determine how to operate them. Another attempt requires a new approach, new information or meaningful experimentation rather than another immediate roll.

Critical failure: the obelisk sends a sudden pulse through the pool. The grasping growth becomes active immediately and remains alert for the next turn; anyone already in the water is attacked.

GM Note
The wave-covered obelisk is the pool's temporary control mechanism. It is useful, but never required; careful players can bypass the pool, improvise a crossing, or simply retreat.

Crossing the water

The pool is about ten feet deep near the western shore and drops quickly into darkness. Apply the campaign's normal swimming rules: half movement, drowning checks by armor and circumstance, and attacks against a swimmer receive the usual +4.

Players are not limited to swimming. Ropes, flotation, poles, magic, improvised rafts or other sensible precautions should matter. A plan that keeps a character out of the water also keeps that character out of reach of the growth.

The island is bait. Up close, the glitter resolves into polished glass, mica, scraps of bright metal, worthless costume stones and a few bent coins too corroded to spend. There is no treasure here. The arrangement is deliberate.

Grasping Seaweed

Aquatic hazard · vine-like tentacle · grapple 1d4 · +4 against swimmers

When an unprotected swimmer passes through the middle of the pool, choose a random eligible target or roll among them. The growth lashes from below and attacks with the normal +4 against a swimmer.

On a hit: the target takes 1d4 damage, is dragged beneath the surface and must make a Strength check each round to keep from being pulled deeper. A successful Strength check breaks the hold. Allies can assist from a rope, the shore or the water as circumstances allow.

Fighting it: underwater attacks suffer the campaign's normal penalties; a dagger attacks at only −2. If the exposed vine takes 4 or more damage from a single attack, it recoils into the depths for 1d4 rounds. It is a hazard, not a monster that needs to be killed.

Behavior: it does not pursue creatures onto land. It catches, constricts and drowns. The worthless island exists to bring prey into reach.

The far shore

A character reaching the eastern passage can secure a rope for others and hears the goblin voices more clearly. The passage bends and reconnects with the route leading toward the chief's chamber in Part VI.

If the party crosses and later wishes to retreat, the pool remains exactly as dangerous unless they successfully operated the obelisk, disabled the growth by some other means, or left a crossing method in place.

Something above

The dragon does not automatically reveal itself the instant somebody enters. It watches.

If the adventurers spend a turn studying the obelisk, disturb the pool, reach the island, cross to the far shore, search the cavern, or otherwise remain long enough to become interesting, use the following reveal when there is a quiet moment:

A faint sizzling comes from the far side of the pool.

Something is dripping into the water from above.

When you raise your light, two green eyes catch it high in the darkness. A young black dragon lies along a shelf of stone near the roof, its glossy scales almost indistinguishable from the shadows around it. Thin threads of acid hang between its teeth and fall one drop at a time into the pool.

It watches you with calm, deliberate intelligence.

Then it draws backward and disappears into the dark.

This is a reveal, not a mandatory combat encounter. Do not roll initiative merely because it has been seen. If the party attacks at range, the dragon uses the height, darkness and rock shelf to withdraw deeper into the complex rather than descending to fight. Its confrontation belongs in Part VI.

If the party enters the cavern, immediately decides the pool is a terrible idea and leaves, let them. The dragon remains unseen. Their first undeniable encounter with it can happen later.

What the chamber tells them

The dragon offers a possible explanation for several things the party has already encountered: unusually well-paid cave sentries, the unnaturally clean pool, and magical resources in goblin hands. It does not explain who carved the fountain, altar or obelisk. Those structures are older than both goblin and dragon occupation.

Do not tell the players which conclusions are correct. Give them the evidence and let them decide what they think is happening.

VTT
Keep the dragon token hidden or do not place one at all. The island should visibly glitter from the western shore. Keep the seaweed hidden until it attacks or is detected through a specific precaution. If the obelisk is activated, visibly mark the pool as safe for one dungeon turn.

Ending Part Five

The chief is still ahead

Part Five ends when the party chooses its route toward the goblin chief: cross the pool and use the eastern shortcut, or backtrack to the Fountain of Destna and take the northwest passage.

Record whether the party discovered the dragon, whether the obelisk was understood, whether the grasping growth was disturbed, and whether a rope or other crossing aid remains in place. These may matter if the party retreats through the complex during Part VI.

No one is required to swim. No one is required to drown. No character is designated to panic, abandon another character, or die here. The pool presents the problem; the table decides what happens.

↑ Contents

Part Six · Finale

You Broke My Toy

Area 6 · the Goblin King · the black gem · and the cave coming down

The Charge

What Part Six is for

The adventurers have finally reached the goblin chief. The confrontation should answer the campaign's central question and immediately replace it with a larger one.

The Goblin King is dangerous, but he is not the true power behind the raids. A black gem sunk into his eye socket has been controlling him. When that control is broken—by death, capture, or destruction of the gem—the thing holding the leash reveals itself.

The young black dragon is not the final combat encounter. It speaks from the high rock shelf, destroys the supports holding up the chamber, and withdraws while the adventurers race for daylight.

GM Snapshot

The adventurers know: the goblin chief is somewhere ahead. They may know he was dying, may have encountered the Stiltwalker, may know what became of Silverlance's alicorn, and may already have seen a young black dragon in the flooded cavern.

What is actually happening: the black gem in the chief's eye is a magical leash. The young dragon has been using the chief and his tribe to farm the frontier for food, loot and tribute while keeping its own existence hidden. It also turned the chief's genuine illness into the unicorn hunt that was meant to remove Silverlance from its claimed territory. The chief's strange pauses and mechanical movements are the visible signs of that control.

This part should reveal: that the Goblin King was being controlled, that the dragon is directly involved in the raids, and that destroying one enemy does not mean the wilderness around Sandpoint is suddenly safe.

Resolve the Alicorn

Pay off the race before the throne-room fight

Part Four deliberately carried forward whether Silverlance's horn ever reached the cave. Resolve that state now.

StateThe Goblin King
The alicorn never reached the caveThe chief is still visibly sick and weakening. Use the Dying King statistics below.
The alicorn reached the cave, but the Stiltwalker did notThe goblins possess the object they needed but lack the shaman who knew the cure. The chief is still sick. The horn or its secured container is somewhere in the throne chamber.
The alicorn and the Stiltwalker both reached the caveThe cure has been completed before the party arrives. Use the Cured King statistics below. The Stiltwalker is present if he survived the earlier chapters and has not left for some other reason.

If the party pursued the fleeing goblins directly and you judge that there was not enough time to finish the cure, begin with the ritual incomplete instead. The horn is present, the king is still dying, and the Stiltwalker becomes part of the encounter.

Map of the Throne Chamber

Area 6 · both routes eventually converge here

▮ pillar▭ crate cover✕ first collapse– – acid breath1 sq = 5 ft.

Four pillars carry the roof. The dragon knows exactly which supports to destroy.

6

The Throne Chamber

The passage climbs into a wide natural cave. Goblin graffiti covers one wall in layers of crude paint and charcoal. Broken furniture, bones and old junk lie everywhere, while battered crates have been dragged into positions that offer cover.

At the back of the chamber stands a throne built from animal bones.

Beside it is a goblin twice the size of the others. A crown of bones and feathers sits above a dark green face dominated by a mouth wide enough to bite through a man's forearm. In one hand he carries a black-bladed sword. A faint silver light moves along its edge as you enter.

Something black and faceted has been sunk deep into one of his eye sockets.

The king looks at you. His head jerks sharply to one side. He goes still for several seconds, listening to something you cannot hear.

Then he smiles.

"Who are these miserable persons?"

Sight
Four guards by default: two near the throne and two behind crates. Four stone pillars rise from floor to ceiling. A dark shelf of rock runs high above the eastern side of the chamber.
Sound
Goblin voices, metal scraping stone, and occasional long silences whenever the king's attention seems to go somewhere else.
Smell
Old bones, spoiled food, smoke and years of habitation. This is a goblin den built inside somebody else's ancient complex.
Feel
The room is tense but not automatically in initiative. Everyone knows violence is close; the players decide whether words come first.

Before initiative

Let the adventurers speak. They may deliver Sandpoint's ultimatum, demand surrender, ask about Silverlance, accuse the king of serving the dragon, offer the alicorn, or attempt something stranger.

The king is not free to accept peace while the gem controls him. Whenever an argument reaches him, describe the same sequence: hesitation, a pulse from the black gem, the king's head jerking toward the high shelf, and sudden renewed hostility. A clever party can understand the problem before anyone swings a weapon.

If the adventurers simply attack, roll initiative normally. If they create a genuine distraction, betrayal or surprise before blades come out, reward it using the campaign's normal surprise rules.

How many goblins are here?

Start with four ordinary goblin guards. Add only survivors who logically escaped earlier encounters and reached the throne room. Cave Alert affects their readiness rather than conjuring extra enemies:

  • Complacent: two guards are sitting or arguing and may be surprised by a quiet approach.
  • Wary: all four are armed and using the crates intelligently.
  • Alarmed: the room knows the adventurers are coming. No automatic surprise is possible, and any earlier survivors are already here.

The Goblin King — Dying

Large goblin · target to hit 13 before bonuses · 2 HD, rolled openly · attack +2 · black blade 1d8 · morale 10 · XP 32

Do not protect a low hit-point roll. If the dice make him fragile, let that be part of the reveal: the terrifying king was a sick puppet propped up by something stronger.

Sneaky. Once per round, when a melee attack hits him and an ordinary goblin is adjacent, the king may drag that goblin into the blow before damage is rolled. The attack damages the unfortunate guard instead. Once the players see this trick, they can prevent it by separating him from his followers.

The Goblin King — Cured

Large goblin · target to hit 13 before bonuses · 3 HD, rolled openly · attack +3 · black blade 1d8+1 · morale 10 · XP 45

Use this version only if both the alicorn and the Stiltwalker reached the cave with enough time to complete the cure. He retains Sneaky and the black gem remains in his eye; curing the disease did nothing to free him.

Goblin Throne Guards (4)

Small humanoid · target to hit 14 before bonuses · 4–7 hp each · attack +1 · hand axe or shortbow 1d6 · morale 7 · XP 7 each

Two use crates for cover if they have time. Two stay close enough to protect the king—and, unknowingly, close enough for him to use as living shields.

If the Stiltwalker is present, use his Part Three statistics. He begins near the throne with any surviving magical resources he still possesses. He knows the party by now and has no reason to waste time explaining himself.

If Norc is present and allied with the adventurers, surviving ordinary goblins make an immediate morale check when the king falls or the gem's control is visibly broken. On a failure they may flee, surrender, or accept Norc's claim rather than fight to the death.

Breaking the leash

The dragon's control ends when the king dies, when he is rendered helpless and the gem is removed, or when the gem itself is successfully destroyed.

Do not require the players to kill the chief if they devise a credible way to subdue him. Removing the gem from a living, resisting king is not a casual action: he must first be restrained, helpless, magically controlled, or otherwise unable to stop the attempt.

The moment the connection is broken, move immediately to The Gem Cracks.

The black blade

The sword is clearly magical and not goblin-made. It glows with a faint silver light in the presence of humans. If recovered, treat it as a +1 longsword for this self-contained module; its origin is deliberately unexplained.

The Gem Cracks

The black gem pulses once.

Again, brighter.

On the third pulse a crack races through it like lightning trapped inside black glass.

A voice enters your thoughts—not loud, but so close that for a moment it feels like your own.

"You broke my toy. Now you will pay."

High above the throne, two green eyes open on the rock shelf.

The young black dragon draws a breath.

Acid lashes across the chamber—not at you, but across two of the pillars holding up the roof.

Stone hisses. A deep crack rolls through the hill.

The dragon turns and disappears along the high ledge as the first rocks begin to fall.

If the party already saw the dragon in Part Five, they recognize it immediately. If not, this is their first undeniable look at what has been watching the goblins from above.

The dragon is not waiting for initiative. It has prepared this escape and knows the chamber better than the adventurers do. Ordinary missile fire may strike stone around it, but it withdraws behind the high shelf as the collapse begins. If the players possess an extraordinary method of reaching, trapping or preventing its escape, let that plan matter; otherwise the dragon leaves.

What the reveal proves: the king was being controlled. The unusual payments to cave sentries and magical resources in goblin hands now have an obvious source. The dragon's involvement with the cursed arrow is strongly suggested, but the adventure does not prove who created the arrow or the black gem.

What can they grab?

There is only a heartbeat between the gem cracking and the escape. Before beginning the challenge below, ask each player whether their character grabs anything immediately within reach: the black blade, the cracked gem or its fragments, the alicorn if it is here, a fallen companion, or nothing at all.

Small objects cost nothing. Carrying a body, chest or similarly awkward burden makes that character's first Escape check hard (−2) unless another character helps.

VTT
Keep the dragon off the combat grid unless the players produce a method that genuinely reaches the high shelf. When the gem cracks, change the scene immediately: mark two pillars destroyed, begin falling-rock effects, and block the pool-side route first.

The Escape

Six successes before three failures

The dragon's acid destabilizes the entire occupied section of the cave. The connection toward the flooded cavern collapses first, forcing the party back through the older rooms toward the moss-covered entrance.

Run the escape as one continuous challenge. Players choose how their characters help; the ability follows from that description, or the description follows from an ability they want to risk. Both approaches are valid.

Escape Challenge

123456
  1. The party needs six successes before three failures.
  2. Any ability may be used except Charisma.
  3. No character may use the same ability twice during the challenge.
  4. Critical successes count as two successes; critical failures count as two failures.
  5. A genuinely hard attempt is made at −2.
  6. Every failed check deals 1 point of falling-rock or impact damage to the acting character in addition to marking a failure.
  7. Animals and noncombatant followers do not need separate checks. They move with the character responsible for them unless the fiction puts them in specific danger.

Three stages

StageWhat is happeningChecks
1. Throne ChamberPillars split, crates tumble, the water-side route vanishes under stone.Up to 3 characters may act before the room becomes impassable.
2. Ancient ComplexDust fills the fountain and altar passages; doors twist in their frames; masonry falls from above.Up to 3 characters may act while the party crosses the old rooms.
3. Entry HollowThe final corridor bucks and sheds stone while daylight shows through the moss curtain ahead.Continue one check at a time until the challenge resolves.

Useful abilities

AbilityExamples
StrengthBrace a falling beam, drag a companion, shove a blocked door open, carry an injured ally.
DexterityVault debris, cross a shifting floor, dive beneath falling stone, get a rope through a narrowing gap.
ConstitutionKeep moving through choking dust, endure heat and impacts, force a path while exhausted.
IntelligenceRecall the dungeon layout, identify the safer arch, recognize which cracked wall will fall next.
WisdomRead the rhythm of the collapse, choose the right moment to cross, notice a companion falling behind.

These are examples, not required stunts. Reward a good idea rather than making the players reproduce anything from another group's escape.

Success

At six successes, the party reaches open air before the final collapse. Award 500 XP to the party for surviving the destruction of the cave.

Three failures

Three failures do not mean that the entire party is automatically buried. They reach the cave mouth as the last section comes down around them. Every character makes a save versus breath weapon. On a failure, take 1d6 falling-rock damage; on a success, avoid the final burst. Characters reduced to 0 or below use the campaign's normal death-and-dying rules.

Survivors still emerge into daylight and earn the 500 XP award. The difference is what the collapse costs them.

Out in the Sunlight

Let the table decide what the victory feels like

You clear the cave mouth and the hillside seems to fold inward behind you.

A wall of dust rolls out through the moss. Stone grinds against stone for several long seconds, then settles into distant cracks and little avalanches.

After the dark, the daylight is almost painful.

The cave is gone.

Do not script the reaction. Count who made it out, who did not, what was carried from the throne room, and what had been left deeper in the complex. Anything still inside when the collapse finishes is buried unless a later adventure deliberately returns to excavate it.

The dragon is gone. The black gem's control has been broken. What remains of the goblin tribe depends on earlier morale, Norc, and how the throne-room fight ended.

Epilogue

Back to Sandpoint

The road home · one report · end of the adventure

The return should be quick. The adventurers know this country now and can follow their own trail back through the hinterlands. Do not restart the Discovery procedure unless they deliberately abandon the known route or create a new problem on the way home.

The first farms appear before Sandpoint itself does.

Work stops as people notice you coming down out of the hills. Someone runs ahead toward town.

By the time you reach the town hall, Mayor Kendra Devron is waiting on the steps.

She looks over the people who came back, then past you toward the road behind.

"Is it over?"

Let the players give the answer. Their report decides what Sandpoint knows about Silverlance, the goblin chief, Norc, the black gem, the dragon, and anyone who did not return.

What changes after the report

  • If the king is dead or the gem's control is broken: the organized raids lose their center. Scattered goblins may remain, but the war against Sandpoint is over.
  • If Norc claims the tribe: any bargain he made with the adventurers begins now. Whether he keeps it belongs to a future campaign.
  • If Silverlance lives: the Meadow of Oaks remains a rare refuge in the wilderness, though he is nobody's tame ally.
  • If anyone was lost: Sandpoint remembers. The shrine will hold a memorial with or without a recovered body.
  • The dragon survives. It knows who broke its puppet and has chosen not to settle that debt today.

Devron pays only rewards or wages actually promised during play. Treasure recovered from the cave can be divided or sold normally.

End here. Sandpoint survived. The goblin war is broken. Somewhere beyond the hills, a young black dragon remembers the adventurers' faces.

↑ Contents

NPC Reference

People and creatures whose choices can change the campaign

These entries describe each NPC before the adventurers determine their fate. Record deaths, alliances, betrayals and other changes at your own table rather than treating any outcome below as fixed.

Employer · Sandpoint

Mayor Kendra Devron

Practical, tired and running out of options. Devron cares more about keeping the farms alive than about glory, revenge or perfect information. She pays what Sandpoint can afford, does not pretend the work is safe, and expects adventurers to return with answers rather than stories polished for her comfort.

Wants: the raids ended, captives returned, and enough stability for the hinterlands to keep feeding the town.

Knows: local raid sites, missing families, roads and farms. She does not know where the chief lives or why the goblins have become desperate.

Captive · Prologue

The Farm Boy (name at the table)

Thin, frightened and determined to get home. He was taken from the fields and has heard goblins whisper about the Skeleton King. A mace hidden in the cage straw is the useful thing he can offer his rescuers.

Wants: out of the warren and back to his family.

Knows: only what he has overheard while imprisoned. He is not a guide to the wider goblin territory.

Goblin runner · Possible claimant

Norc

Quick-thinking, frightened of the Stiltwalker, and ambitious enough to recognize an opportunity when the adventurers create one. Norc is useful because he knows the tribe; he is dangerous because he wants something from it.

Wants: to survive first, then replace the current chief if a believable path to the throne appears.

Knows: the chief is dying, the Stiltwalker seeks a unicorn's horn, Silverlance was wounded, and a war band is searching northeast. If Norc remains involved long enough, he can also identify the politics of the chief's cave.

Promise: if the adventurers help clear his path to leadership, he may promise to end the raids on Sandpoint. He means it when he says it; whether ambition changes him later is outside this adventure.

Unicorn · Meadow of Oaks

Silverlance

An old unicorn, physically imposing even when badly wounded. Silverlance communicates telepathically, speaks little, and responds more to conduct than persuasion. He recognizes protection, restraint and genuine healing; he does not regard himself as treasure or as a weapon to be recruited.

Wants: the cursed arrow removed, the hunt ended, and his meadow left alone.

Knows: goblins wounded and hunted him, and the arrow carried hostile magic. He does not know the internal politics of the tribe or the origin of the black gem.

If saved: he restores living creatures in the meadow to full hit points and rewards the rescue as described in Part III.

Enemies & Hazards

Neutral reference · outcomes belong to your table

"Target to hit" is the unmodified roll used by this module before the attacking character's bonuses. Where the adventure gives a full Dragonslayer Armor Class, use the normal system value instead. Encounter entries remain authoritative if a local version differs from this summary.

Goblin

Small humanoid · AC 6 · target to hit 14 · 4–7 hp · attack +1 · hand axe, spear or shortsword 1d6 · morale 7 · XP 7

Uses cover, high ground and flanking whenever possible. Goblins are frightened easily but become vicious around helpless targets. Check morale once half the group is down.

Goblin Boss

Small humanoid · target to hit 14 · 7–9 hp · attack +2 · hand axe 1d6+1 · XP 14

Keeps discipline through intimidation and targets enemies already in trouble. If the boss falls, make an immediate morale check for ordinary goblins.

Wolf

Medium beast · target to hit 13 · 12 hp · bite 1d6 · XP 36

Howls or scent-hunts before charging. An attack roll of 18–20 also knocks the target prone. It attacks the nearest obvious threat rather than planning like a humanoid.

Orc

Medium humanoid · target to hit 14 · 4–6 hp · shortsword, spear or bow 1d6 · XP 9 · appears 2d4

Prefers ambush, split approaches and poorly armored targets. Check morale once half the group is down.

Orc Leader

Medium humanoid · target to hit 14 · 6–8 hp · sword and shield · XP 9

Stays just behind the first rush and gives orders. If the leader falls, immediately check morale for the remaining orcs.

Giant Spitting Beetle

Medium beast · appears 1d3 · caustic spit · use standard Dragonslayer creature statistics

Always roll activity and reaction before deciding that the beetles attack. A favorable reaction may leave them curious, territorial or simply avoidable.

Goblin Champion

Small humanoid · target to hit 14 · 8 hp · attack +2 · good hand axe 1d6+1 · morale 9

The physical enforcer beneath the Stiltwalker. He commits hard to melee and props up the courage of ordinary goblins; his fall triggers a morale check.

The Stiltwalker (goblin shaman)

Small humanoid on wooden stilts · target to hit 14 · 7 hp · club 1d6 · spellcaster

A small goblin built into an absurd six-foot figure with stilts, wooden arm extensions, filthy furs and a hollow pumpkin helmet. His contraption is awkward in dense brush.

Entangle: roots and grass seize a broad area, affecting goblins and adventurers alike. Failed saves immobilize; successful saves allow half movement; entangled creatures are attacked at +4.

Cause light wounds: save versus spells or suffer 1d8+1 damage from black unholy fire.

Cave Sentry (goblin)

Use common goblin statistics

In a Complacent cave, the sentries are drunk and inattentive. Wary or Alarmed sentries use cover and watch the entrance properly. Their unusual gold payment is a clue, not a statistical difference.

Baby Giant Black Widow

Medium beast · target to hit 14 · 1 HD · bite 1d4 + paralysis · surprise on d4 · appears 3

Ambushes from above and lands among the party rather than politely at the room's edge. These juveniles paralyze rather than inflict the adult widow's lethal venom. Roll targets rather than making them tacticians.

Grasping Seaweed (hazard)

Aquatic hazard · grapple · 1d4 damage · +4 against swimmers

A thick vine seizes a swimmer, drags the victim under and forces a Strength check each round to remain at the surface or break free. Strong attacks can drive it back temporarily. The Obelisk of Waves can quiet the growth for one dungeon turn.

The Statues of Humility (hazard)

Flame trap · 2d6 fire · save versus breath weapon for half

The warning is literal: those who cross upright trigger the flames; those who approach kneeling or crawling pass safely. The statues may be disabled, but bypassing the lesson is intentionally harder than understanding it.

The Goblin King — Dying

Large goblin · target to hit 13 · 2 HD, rolled openly · attack +2 · black blade 1d8 · morale 10 · XP 32

Sneaky: once per round, when a melee attack hits him and an ordinary goblin is adjacent, he may drag that goblin into the blow before damage is rolled. The guard takes the hit instead. Separating him from followers prevents this.

The Goblin King — Cured

Large goblin · target to hit 13 · 3 HD, rolled openly · attack +3 · black blade 1d8+1 · morale 10 · XP 45

Use only if both the alicorn and the Stiltwalker reached the cave with time to complete the cure. He retains Sneaky. The black gem still controls him; curing the disease does not free him.

The Skeleton King

Medium undead · target to hit 12 · 14 hp · attack +2 · longsword 1d8+1

Self-summoning golden plate forms as he rises. Bludgeoning attacks gain +4 to hit; alternatively, halve slashing damage if you prefer to express the same weakness as resistance. At 0 hp the armor vanishes and the bones become dust.

The Young Black Dragon

Future threat · acid breath · telepathic voice · high ledges and prepared escape routes

A cruel, territorial young dragon establishing its first serious claim. It prefers puppets, paid guards, ambushes and prepared exits to any fair fight. The goblin tribe is useful because it can raid Sandpoint, gather tribute and die on the dragon's behalf without advertising that a dragon has moved into the region.

Part V and Part VI use the dragon as an environmental antagonist rather than a level-appropriate combat encounter. If the adventurers somehow force a true fight, use the normal Dragonslayer young black dragon statistics rather than weakening it to fit the party.

Experience

Award normal Dragonslayer experience for monsters and hazards defeated, routed, captured or otherwise overcome. Avoiding a dangerous encounter through successful play counts as overcoming it. Do not keep a fixed campaign total: the Discovery race, random encounters, retreats, alliances and casualties can all change what a group actually faces.

ObjectiveAward
Saving Silverlance650 XP
Escaping the collapsing cave500 XP
Goblin King — dying version32 XP
Goblin King — cured version45 XP
Throne guards7 XP each

Expected advancement: begin at 1st level. Most groups should be approaching or reaching 2nd level during Parts II–III and should enter the final cave as seasoned 1st-level or 2nd-level survivors. Exact timing depends on class XP requirements, random encounters, treasure conversion and which objectives the party actually completes.

Loose Ends

Optional hooks beyond The Black Eye of the Goblin King

None of these questions must be answered for this adventure to feel complete. They are deliberately left behind for a referee who wants Sandpoint to remain a campaign rather than a single arc.

Prologue · Unanswered

Who crowned the Skeleton King?

The warren contains an articulate undead monarch with self-summoning golden armor, a jeweled throne and no connection to the goblins occupying the upper tunnels. His crown leaves nothing behind when he falls. He may be a completely separate mystery—or the first evidence that old things beneath Sandpoint are waking up.

Parts III–VI · Unanswered

Who made the cursed arrow and the black gem?

The young dragon supplied the cursed arrow and uses the black gem to control the Goblin King. That much is now settled. Their manufacture is not. Both are more sophisticated than anything the goblins could produce, and the dragon may have stolen, traded for, inherited or discovered them in the old complex. Their maker remains available as a future mystery.

Parts IV–VI · Buried

Who built the old complex?

The goblins did not carve Destna's fountain, consecrate the Altar of Humility, raise the Obelisk of Waves, hang proper doors, or cut the older worked passages. The dragon behaves like a tenant rather than an architect: when threatened, it destroys the place and leaves. The builders remain unknown beneath the collapsed hill.

Part VI · At large

The young black dragon

The dragon wanted three things: Silverlance gone, the frontier feeding its growing hoard, and its claimed lair left undisturbed. The adventurers may have taken all three away from it.

Its puppet is gone and its lair is damaged, but the dragon survives. It knows the adventurers' faces and considers the loss personal. It will not seek an honorable rematch. It can attack Sandpoint through new minions, poison alliances, steal something the adventurers value, establish another hidden lair, or simply disappear for months or years before collecting what it believes it is owed.

Variable · Political

Who leads the surviving goblins?

If Norc survives and makes his bid, he may inherit a broken tribe and a bargain with Sandpoint. If he is absent, dead or rejected, another survivor eventually fills the vacuum. Ending the war does not require exterminating every goblin in the hills; it changes who has the power to start the next one.

Variable · Silverlance

The alicorn and the Meadow of Oaks

If Silverlance lives, his meadow remains a place of power and a reason for dangerous people to return. If he dies, the fate of his horn may matter long after the goblin chief is gone. Track where the alicorn actually ended up rather than assuming the campaign forgets it.

Buried · Not necessarily destroyed

What survived the collapse?

The fountain, altar, pool, obelisk, throne room and deeper passages are buried, not erased. A collapsed hillside is a serious obstacle, but it is not a magical seal. Excavation, underground water, another entrance or something digging outward can reopen the old complex whenever the campaign needs it.

Appendix: Additional Campaign Rulings

Situational rules that do not need to live in the referee's head

  • Coup de grâce. An attack on a helpless target hits automatically; the target saves versus death or dies.
  • Fighting withdrawal. A character may disengage from melee as their action and may shift one square to seek a better position.
  • Track rations. Strike one per meal, or use usage dice below. Hunger should matter only when time and distance make supplies meaningful.
  • Usage dice. The ladder is d20 → d12 → d10 → d8 → d6 → d4 → gone. Roll when the resource is meaningfully used; on 1–2 step down one die. A 1–2 on d4 exhausts it. Suggested starts: torches d6, rations d8, arrows d10, oil d8, holy water d4.
  • Potions. Potions last four turns unless their entry says otherwise. A cautious small sip identifies one without consuming the dose.
  • Trap work can backfire. A dangerous trap may have a second failure threshold that actually triggers it. State the danger through the fiction before the roll.
  • Ambush predators. Creatures dropping from ceilings or striking from prepared concealment surprise on a d4 when the encounter says so.
  • Large targets. Especially large creatures may be one or two points easier to hit than smaller creatures of the same kind.
  • Shooting into melee. Missile fire into a tight scrum risks striking an ally. Resolve the risk before the attack is rolled or use your normal Dragonslayer method.
  • Touch spells can be interrupted. A caster hit before delivering a declared touch spell loses the spell.
  • Hirelings face the same danger. Use the same death-and-dying rules for named hirelings and animal companions unless their entry says otherwise.
  • Wisdom notices; Intelligence searches. Use Wisdom when something may be noticed incidentally and Intelligence when a character deliberately studies or hunts for it.
  • Swimming. Move at half speed. Drowning risk rises sharply with armor; heavy armor is generally a problem to solve rather than a percentage gamble. Attacks against swimmers gain +4. Underwater dagger attacks are made at −2.
  • Funeral offerings. If using the campaign's memorial rule, gold voluntarily offered for a fallen companion converts to experience rather than remaining spendable wealth. A memorial without a recovered body still qualifies.
  • Secret thief rolls. Roll stealth, trap and similar thief skills behind the screen when failure would not be immediately obvious to the character.
  • Cleave. A fighter who kills with an attack may immediately strike an adjacent enemy.
  • Food can heal. A substantial field meal may restore 1d3 hp when the referee wants food to function as a meaningful resource.
  • Battle fury die (optional). Set out a d6. Each missed attack raises the tally by one; add the tally to the next attack, then reset it after a hit.
  • No electrum. Convert electrum treasure to silver.

Appendix: The Tables

Ten ready tables used or referenced by the module

Use these when the adventure calls for a wilderness creature, activity, reaction, random find, potion, oddity or blessing. If your Dragonslayer table already has an equivalent you prefer, substitute it freely.

2 · What it is doing when you find it

d10Activity
1Hunting, and it has your scent already
2Eating a kill — recent, and possibly someone you know
3Asleep
4On the move with somewhere to be
5Fighting among themselves
6Digging, building or nesting
7Drinking heavily — grant surprise bonuses accordingly
8Wounded and desperate
9Guarding something worth guarding
10Socialising or playing

3 · Reaction

RollReaction
0–6Attacks immediately, no roll needed
7–8May attack — provoke it and it will
9Fifty-fifty; roll for it
10–12Curious but not hostile — avoidable if you give it room
13+Indifferent or friendly; may be talked to

A favorable reaction does not make a dangerous creature tame. It means the encounter can be handled without violence. Award normal encounter experience when the party successfully overcomes or avoids a real danger through play.

4 · Death and dying

Hit pointsWhat happens
Exactly 0Unconscious for 1d6 rounds, then revives at 1 hp. Roll the duration in the open.
−1 to −6Unconscious and dying. Save versus death: success means stable but out of the fight.
−7 to −10Save versus death at a penalty; success leaves them alive but needing magic to wake.
Below −10Dead outright, no save.
Natural 20A miracle — the character stands at 1 hit point. Applies to animals too.

Use each character's normal save versus death. Named hirelings use the same chart unless their entry says otherwise. A coup de grâce against a helpless target hits automatically and forces the save.

5 · Critical miss

d6Result
1You drop your weapon; recovering it costs your movement
2You fall prone — and prone characters are attacked at +4
3You lose your footing: −2 to hit next round
4A strap or buckle fails: −1 armour until ten minutes' repair
5You overextend — your target gets an immediate free attack
6Something in your kit gives out: step one usage die down

When a monster rolls a natural 1, skip this table: the character it attacked gets an immediate free hack instead.

6 · Morale

CreatureMorale
Goblins7
Goblin boss, champion or shaman9
Orcs8
Animals and vermin6
Predators defending a kill or a nest9
Hirelings5
Undead and the controllednever checks

Roll a d10 against the score: equal or higher and the creature flees. Check when half the group is down, when the leader falls, or when something happens that would frighten anybody. Roll it in the open — a goblin that passes and fights on surrounded tells the players something about what it is more afraid of at home.

10 · Destna's blessing

d10Blessing · one gold coin, dropped in and drunk
1–3+1 armour class for your next combat
4–5+1 to attacks for your next combat
6–7Reroll one failed saving throw today
8+2 armour class for your next combat
9+2 to attacks for your next combat
10+2 to attacks, saves and armour class — your choice of emphasis — until the end of the adventure
